docs.text:
Flaskteroids is a Python MVC framework built on Flask, SQLAlchemy, and Celery. It uses Rails 8 as the reference for its conventions and framework behavior.

The framework chooses an application layout and discovers models, controllers, and templates in their conventional directories. It includes resource routing, database migrations, form helpers, background jobs, and email delivery. Flask APIs and extensions remain available when you need them.

Generators create models, controllers, scaffolds, mailers, and authentication code. Applications include environment-specific settings, encrypted credentials, and pytest-based tests with YAML fixtures and transactional rollback. Browser tests use Playwright.

Start with Getting started to build a product catalog, learn the MVC workflow, and add authentication, uploads, email, and tests.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
• Project structure and configuration explain where files live and how an application boots.
  • The models guide covers associations, validations, callbacks, and queries.
  • Controllers and routing cover request handling and HTML or JSON responses.
  • Views and forms cover templates and form submissions.
  • Testing covers model, integration, job, mailer, and browser tests.
  • The CLI reference lists generators and credentials commands.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Configure application-wide settings in config/application.py and override them in config/environments/. Database settings live in config/database.yml. Store secrets in encrypted credentials and use initializers to configure external libraries during boot.

docs.title: Application settings
docs.text:
Start with config/application.py for settings shared by every environment:

from flaskteroids.application import Application as FlaskteroidsApplication
from config.boot import ROOT


class Application(FlaskteroidsApplication):
    root = ROOT

    def configure(self, config):
        config.load_defaults('0.1')
        config.x.payments.provider = 'stripe'

config.load_defaults() selects the framework defaults for the given version. Updating Flaskteroids does not change that selection. Change the version passed to load_defaults() to adopt newer defaults.

docs.title: Template helpers
docs.text:
Application helpers are discovered in app.helpers and included in controller views by default:

config.paths.helpers = "app.helpers"
config.action_controller.include_all_helpers = True

Set include_all_helpers = False to include only ApplicationHelper, conventionally matching controller helpers, and explicit helper(...) selections. See application helpers for inheritance, naming, mailer boundaries, and development reloading.

docs.title: Request limits
docs.text:
Set request limits in configure, rather than in request or controller callbacks:

config["MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"] = 16 * 1024 * 1024  # Total request body: 16 MiB
config["MAX_FORM_MEMORY_SIZE"] = 500_000         # Each multipart text field
config["MAX_FORM_PARTS"] = 1_000                # Multipart fields and files

Requests that exceed these limits are rejected with 413 Content Too Large.

docs.title: Using models and jobs in scripts
docs.text:
Requests and jobs run inside an application context. In scripts, open one before using models or enqueueing jobs:

from config.environment import application

with application.app_context():
    user = User.find(1)
    MyJob().perform_later(user_id=user.id)

Each context has its own database session, but is not itself a transaction. Standalone model persistence commits before returning. Use with Model.transaction(): to group operations; an escaping exception rolls that group back. Context exit rolls back unfinished work and closes the session, without undoing earlier standalone commits. Native writes require explicit commit/transaction handling. See Models.

docs.title: Environments
docs.text:
Flaskteroids selects the environment in this order:

  1. The explicit environment= argument to Application.initialize().
  2. FLASK_ENV.
  3. development.

Flaskteroids reads FLASK_ENV to select configuration. Flask itself no longer uses this variable; use flask run --debug to enable its debugger.

Flaskteroids applies the selected file under config/environments/ after application-wide configuration:

# config/environments/production.py
import os


def configure(config):
    config.eager_load = True
    config.consider_all_requests_local = False
    config.require_master_key = True
    config.action_mailer.perform_deliveries = True
    config.active_job.broker_url = os.environ.get(
        'CELERY_BROKER_URL', config.active_job.broker_url
    )

The current environment is available from the application:

application.env.name
application.env.development
application.env.test
application.env.production

Read other environment variables with os.environ in your configuration.

docs.title: Database configuration
docs.text:
Define database connections in config/database.yml:

default: &default
  adapter: sqlite3
  pool: 5

development:
  <<: *default
  database: storage/development.sqlite3

test:
  <<: *default
  database: storage/test.sqlite3

production:
  url: ${DATABASE_URL}

The generated app uses SQLite for development and tests. For another database, install its driver and set DATABASE_URL:

For PostgreSQL:

uv add 'psycopg[binary]'
export DATABASE_URL='postgresql+psycopg://app:password@localhost/my_app'

Or for MySQL:

uv add 'PyMySQL[rsa]'
export DATABASE_URL='mysql+pymysql://app:password@localhost/my_app'

YAML values can reference environment variables with ${NAME} or ${NAME:-default}. Connection settings are chosen in this order:

  1. An explicit url in database.yml.
  2. DATABASE_URL.
  3. Individual settings such as adapter, database, username, and password.

docs.title: Preparing for deployment
docs.text:
On a fresh checkout, run bin/setup to install dependencies and prepare the database. Before deploying database changes, prepare your production environment:

FLASK_ENV=production bin/flask db:prepare

Start PostgreSQL or MySQL yourself and give the application permission to create its database. If your host provisions it for you, use db:migrate to apply changes. PostgreSQL preparation also needs access to the postgres database; choose another with config.database_tasks.maintenance_database if your host requires it. See database commands for the everyday workflow.

Provide FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY when starting production so the app can read its encrypted credentials. Keep the key out of your image and source control. SQLite databases and local uploads need persistent storage.

The generated Docker setup prepares the database before starting the web app. When deploying several instances, arrange one release step for migrations instead of letting every instance run them. Your generated deploy/README.md walks through that setup.

docs.title: Encrypted credentials
docs.text:
Shared credentials live in config/credentials.yml.enc. Flaskteroids stores the local encryption key in config/master.key. Generated Git and container ignore files exclude the key.

Edit or display credentials with:

flask credentials:edit
flask credentials:show

Environment-specific credentials use the --environment option:

flask credentials:edit --environment production
flask credentials:show --environment production

These commands create:

config/credentials/production.yml.enc
config/credentials/production.key

When environment-specific credentials exist, they replace the shared credentials for that environment. Flaskteroids reads the encryption key from FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY first, then from the corresponding key file.

Credentials are available through the application:

application.credentials.secret_key_base
application.credentials.payments.api_key
application.credentials['payments']['api_key']

secret_key_base signs sessions, CSRF tokens, and password-reset tokens. Production should set config.require_master_key = True so boot fails when credentials cannot be decrypted.

docs.title: Initializers
docs.text:
Put startup configuration for external libraries in config/initializers/:

# config/initializers/payments.py
from flaskteroids import application
from payments import Client

application.extensions['payments'] = Client(
    api_key=application.credentials.payments.api_key
)

Keep database queries out of initializers when possible. Query from an action, job, or function when the data is needed, so database setup can run before tables exist.

docs.title: Getting started with Flaskteroids
docs.text:
This guide walks you through building a small product catalog called store. You will create records, display them in a browser, build forms, require login for changes, and attach product images. Then you'll track stock and let visitors subscribe to an email when a sold-out product becomes available again.

By the end, you will know how to:

  • Create and run a Flaskteroids application.
  • Work with models, migrations, and validations.
  • Follow a request through routes, controllers, and views.
  • Build a complete create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) interface.
  • Add authentication, uploads, associations, and inventory tracking.
  • Connect model callbacks to background restock emails and unsubscribe links.
  • Test your application and prepare it for deployment.

You need basic Python and HTML knowledge, but no prior experience with Flask, SQLAlchemy, or Celery. The examples introduce Flaskteroids APIs and conventions as you build the application.

docs.title: 1. The Flaskteroids approach
docs.text:
Flaskteroids is a Python MVC framework built with Flask, SQLAlchemy, and Celery. It gives these components a shared application structure and workflow. Two ideas guide that workflow:

  • Convention over configuration: names and directories tell the framework where your models, controllers, templates, and jobs belong.
  • Don't repeat yourself: migrations describe database structure; models describe behavior; reusable templates and callbacks keep shared logic together.

You can use the underlying libraries when needed, but ordinary application work should not require managing ORM mappings or database sessions yourself.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install these tools before continuing:

  • Python 3.12 or newer.
  • Git and Bash.
  • uv.
  • A code editor.

The shell commands in this guide assume a POSIX environment, such as Linux, macOS, or Windows through WSL. SQLite is included with Python; you do not need a separate database server for this tutorial.

Start by creating and activating a virtual environment, then install Flaskteroids:

python3 -m venv flaskteroids-env
source flaskteroids-env/bin/activate
pip install flaskteroids

Generate your application in a new directory:

flaskteroids new store
cd store

The generator creates the project, installs its dependencies with uv into its own .venv, and prepares the development database. It also creates encrypted credentials and a local master key.

From now on, run commands inside store, using bin/flask. This wrapper uses the application's virtual environment automatically, so you do not need to activate it in each terminal. You can explore commands with:

bin/flask --help
bin/flask generate --help

If you used flaskteroids new store --skip-install, run bin/setup before continuing. Use that same setup command on a fresh checkout. Commit uv.lock so other developers and deployment builds use the same dependency versions. Never commit config/master.key.

docs.title: A quick directory tour
docs.text:
Open the generated directory in your editor:

Path Purpose app/models/ Data behavior, validations, and associations. app/controllers/ Actions that handle requests. app/views/ Jinja HTML and email templates. app/helpers/ Reusable template helpers. app/mailers/, app/jobs/ Email actions and background work. app/assets/ Stylesheets, images, and other source assets. config/routes.py URL-to-action mappings. config/database.yml Database connections by environment. config/environments/ Development, test, and production settings. db/migrate/ Database migration history. db/schema.py Generated snapshot of the migrated database. test/ Tests and fixtures. storage/ Local databases and uploaded files. bin/ Application commands and setup/release scripts. deploy/README.md Generated Docker and deployment instructions.

See Project structure for the complete layout.

docs.title: Model, view, controller
docs.text:
Most of our work will happen in three places:

  • A model represents application data and its rules: a Product, for example.
  • A controller handles a request, loads or changes data, and chooses a response.
  • A view turns the controller's data into HTML.

Routes connect a browser's request to the right controller action. We will build all of these pieces rather than start with a scaffold, so you can see how they fit together.

docs.title: 3. Hello, Flaskteroids!
docs.text:
Start the development server:

bin/flask run --debug

Open http://127.0.0.1:5000. You should see the Flaskteroids welcome page. This confirms that the generated application boots and serves requests.

Keep the server in one terminal and run other commands in another terminal in store. Press Ctrl-C to stop the server. Debug mode reloads changed Python code and provides an interactive debugger; use it only on your own development machine.

Flaskteroids discovers components in their conventional directories. Python imports are still explicit: a controller imports the models it uses. After migrations, stop and restart the server so it loads the new schema snapshot.

docs.title: 4. Create a product model
docs.text:
Stop the server and generate a model:

bin/flask generate model Product name:string description:text

This creates:

  • app/models/product.py: the behavioral model.
  • A migration under db/migrate/versions/: instructions for creating the table.
  • test/models/product_test.py: a starting point for model tests.

Use singular CamelCase for model names. Product maps to the plural table products by convention.

docs.title: Understand the migration
docs.text:
Open the generated migration. Its upgrade() function creates products with name and description columns, an integer primary key id, and timestamps created_at and updated_at. Its downgrade() function drops the table.

Migrations record structural changes so every environment can apply them in order. Review generated migrations before running them, especially when removing data or adding constraints.

Apply the migration:

bin/flask db:migrate

db:migrate applies pending migrations and regenerates db/schema.py. The application generator already prepared the development database. The generated database configuration uses storage/development.sqlite3 for development and a separate database for tests.

Open app/models/product.py:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    pass

An empty model is useful! Its mapped attributes come from the schema snapshot. We add application behavior here without repeating its column definitions.

Commit migrations and db/schema.py, but do not edit the snapshot by hand. Future database changes belong in new migrations. bin/flask db:rollback undoes the most recent migration; a rollback that drops data cannot recover that data.

docs.title: 5. Work with records in the shell
docs.text:
Before building pages, let's see what a product can do. Open the application shell:

bin/flask shell

The shell provides an application context and makes your models available automatically. You can use Product directly. In the examples below, >>> is the Python prompt, not something to type; the lines without it show the result.

docs.title: Create and query
docs.text:
Build a product and save it:

>>> product = Product.new(name="T-Shirt", description="A comfortable cotton shirt.")
>>> product.save()
True
>>> product.name
'T-Shirt'

new() builds an unsaved object. save() validates and persists it, returning True on success. The database assigns product.id when the record is saved. Create another product with the combined build-and-save operation:

>>> pants = Product.create(name="Pants", description="Everyday trousers.")
>>> Product.count()
2
>>> [item.name for item in Product.all()]
['T-Shirt', 'Pants']

create() returns the object, including when validation fails. Later we will use its errors to explain unsuccessful saves.

Find and filter records:

>>> Product.find(product.id).name
'T-Shirt'
>>> Product.find_by(name="Pants").description
'Everyday trousers.'
>>> [item.name for item in Product.where(name="Pants").order(name="asc")]
['Pants']

find() raises RecordNotFoundException if the record is absent; find_by() returns None. all() and where() return lazy queries: iteration loads the records. Keep the returned query when chaining filters or ordering.

docs.title: Update and delete
docs.text:
Change the shirt's name, then try assigning and saving a description separately:

>>> product.update(name="Cotton T-Shirt")
True
>>> product.description = "Available in several colors."
>>> product.save()
True

Assignments alone do not save a record. A standalone save(), create(), update(), or destroy() commits before returning; no extra session or commit call is needed. See Models when several operations need to succeed together.

Create a temporary product and delete it:

>>> temporary = Product.create(name="Sample", description="For this example only.")
>>> temporary.destroy()
True
>>> Product.count()
2

The temporary record is gone, while our shirt and pants remain. We'll use those products when we build the catalog page.

docs.title: Add validation
docs.text:
A product without a name would be hard to browse. Exit the shell with exit(), then replace app/models/product.py with:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import validates


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    validates("name", presence=True)

Declarations such as validations, associations, and callbacks go directly inside the class body, with explicit imports. This validation requires a nonblank name. It changes behavior, not database structure, so there is no migration to run.

Open a new bin/flask shell to load the edited model:

>>> product = Product.new(name="", description="Still available for redisplay.")
>>> product.save()
False
>>> bool(product.errors)
True
>>> product.description
'Still available for redisplay.'

Run product.errors.full_messages() to read the validation messages. Notice that the object still holds the entered description. That will let us redisplay a form without making the visitor type everything again.

Fix the name and retry:

>>> product.name = "Socks"
>>> product.save()
True

Exit with exit(). Your development database now has three products: Cotton T-Shirt, Pants, and Socks. Next, let's give them a home on the web.

docs.title: 6. Follow a request through the application
docs.text:
Our product data exists, but it has no web interface yet. A page request follows this path:

GET /products
  → config/routes.py
  → ProductsController.index()
  → Product.all()
  → app/views/products/index.html
  → HTML response

docs.title: Define resource routes
docs.text:
Replace config/routes.py with:

def register(route):
    route.get("/up/", to="flaskteroids/health#show")
    route.root(to="products#index")
    route.resources("products")

Keep the generated /up/ health route and the parameter name route, which other generators use when adding routes. The root route makes the catalog our home page. resources() creates the standard CRUD routes:

Method Path Action Purpose GET /products index List products. GET /products/new new Display a creation form. POST /products create Save a new product. GET /products/<int:id> show Display one product. GET /products/<int:id>/edit edit Display an editing form. PUT/PATCH /products/<int:id> update Save changes. DELETE /products/<int:id> destroy Delete a product.

GET retrieves information. POST creates it, PUT/PATCH updates it, and DELETE removes it. Helpers generate slashless resource URLs. A trailing slash is also accepted without redirecting or replaying a request body.

Inspect the application's routes with:

bin/flask routes

Routes identify actions with "controller#action": products#index means ProductsController.index. The framework discovers that class in app/controllers/products_controller.py.

docs.title: Generate a controller
docs.text:
bin/flask generate controller Products index --skip-routes

The generator creates a controller, helper, index template, and controller test. --skip-routes avoids adding routes because we already defined them.

Replace app/controllers/products_controller.py with:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.product import Product


class ProductsController(ApplicationController):
    def index(self):
        self.products = Product.all()

When an action returns None, Flaskteroids renders its matching template. Controller instance variables become template variables: self.products is available as products.

Replace app/views/products/index.html with:

{% extends "layouts/application.html" %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>Products</h1>
  <ul>
    {% for product in products %}
      <li>{{ product.name }}</li>
    {% else %}
      <li>No products yet.</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
{% endblock %}

Jinja's {% ... %} tags control the template, while {{ ... }} outputs a value. The layout supplies the surrounding HTML; this template fills its body block.

Run bin/flask run --debug again and visit http://127.0.0.1:5000. You should see the products you created in the shell.

docs.title: 7. Build the CRUD interface
docs.text: The catalog lists product names, but visitors cannot open a product yet. We'll add that first, then create products in the browser, edit them, and finally remove them. Keep the existing controller actions as you add each new one.

docs.title: Show a product
docs.text:
In app/controllers/products_controller.py, add a show action:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.product import Product


class ProductsController(ApplicationController):
    def index(self):
        self.products = Product.all()

    def show(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["id"])

The resource route captures the ID from /products/<int:id>. The show action finds that product and makes it available to its template as product.

Create app/views/products/show.html:

{% extends "layouts/application.html" %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>{{ product.name }}</h1>
  <p>{{ product.description }}</p>
  {{ link_to("Back", products_path()) }}
{% endblock %}

Now give visitors a way to reach it. In app/views/products/index.html, replace <li>{{ product.name }}</li> with:

<li>{{ link_to(product.name, product_path(product)) }}</li>

link_to builds a link. Resource helpers such as product_path(product) have the same meaning in templates and Python; import them from flaskteroids.routes in Python code. Native Flask url_for remains available for custom endpoint-based routing.

Try it: refresh the catalog, click Cotton T-Shirt, and follow Back. You can now browse both the collection and an individual product without typing its ID.

docs.title: Extract a presentation helper
docs.text:
Move reusable presentation logic into app/helpers/products_helper.py. If the controller generator already created this file, replace its empty class:

class ProductsHelper:
    def product_link(self, product):
        return self.link_to(product.name, self.product_path(product))

In app/views/products/index.html, the product list item can now be:

<li>{{ product_link(product) }}</li>

Helper classes are loaded automatically: no controller import or callback is needed. Inside a helper, self provides the shared view context, including other helpers and route helpers. Ordinary strings are escaped; link_to returns safely constructed HTML. See application helpers for helper selection and inheritance.

docs.title: Create products in the browser
docs.text:
So far we have created products in the shell. A web form needs two actions: new displays it, and create processes its submission.

Add this import to the controller:

from flaskteroids.routes import product_path

Add these methods inside ProductsController, keeping index and show:

    def new(self):
        self.product = Product.new()

    def create(self):
        self.product = Product.new(**self._product_params())
        if self.product.save():
            return self.redirect_to(product_path(self.product))
        return self.render("new", status=422)

    def _product_params(self):
        return self.params.expect(product=["name", "description"])

Create app/views/products/new.html:

{% extends "layouts/application.html" %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>New product</h1>
  {% call(form) form_with(model=product) %}
    {% if product.errors %}
      <ul class="errors">
        {% for message in product.errors.full_messages() %}
          <li>{{ message }}</li>
        {% endfor %}
      </ul>
    {% endif %}

    <div>
      {{ form.label("name") }}
      {{ form.text_field("name") }}
    </div>
    <div>
      {{ form.label("description") }}
      {{ form.text_area("description") }}
    </div>
    {{ form.submit("Save product") }}
  {% endcall %}
  {{ link_to("Cancel", products_path()) }}
{% endblock %}

form_with(model=product) chooses the creation URL, includes a CSRF token, and fills its inputs from the model. The generated field names put the submission inside a product object.

Our _product_params() method uses self.params.expect() to require that outer object and select only name and description. It does not require every listed field to be present. Never pass unfiltered request data to a model: visitors can submit attributes that your HTML form does not expose.

After the heading in app/views/products/index.html, add:

{{ link_to("New product", new_product_path()) }}

Try it: click New product and create a product named Hat. You should land on its show page. Follow Back and check that Hat appears in the catalog.

docs.title: Help visitors correct mistakes
docs.text:
Open New product again. Enter a description, leave the name blank, and save. You should stay on the form, see a validation message, and keep your description.

That happens because create renders new with status 422 when saving fails. Rendering reuses the invalid product, including its errors and entered values. A redirect would start a new request and lose that state.

Enter a name and save again. The same form now succeeds. We have connected the validation we tried in the shell to a useful browser experience.

docs.title: Edit an existing product
docs.text:
Editing has the same two-part shape: edit displays a form and update saves its submission. Add these methods to ProductsController:

    def edit(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["id"])

    def update(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["id"])
        if self.product.update(**self._product_params()):
            return self.redirect_to(product_path(self.product))
        return self.render("edit", status=422)

We could copy the creation form, but then every new field would need two edits. Instead, move the complete {% call(form) form_with(model=product) %} block, through its {% endcall %}, from new.html into a new file: app/views/products/_form.html.

The underscore marks this as a reusable partial. Replace new.html with:

{% extends "layouts/application.html" %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>New product</h1>
  {% include "products/_form.html" %}
  {{ link_to("Cancel", products_path()) }}
{% endblock %}

Create app/views/products/edit.html:

{% extends "layouts/application.html" %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>Edit product</h1>
  {% include "products/_form.html" %}
  {{ link_to("Cancel", product_path(product)) }}
{% endblock %}

Both includes receive the current product. For a persisted record, form_with chooses its member URL and PATCH. The helper renders a POST form with a hidden PATCH override because browsers submit only GET or POST directly. An explicit method="PUT" is supported, but PATCH is the inferred update method.

After the Back link in app/views/products/show.html, add:

{{ link_to("Edit", edit_product_path(product)) }}

Try it: edit Hat, change its description, and save. Then try an edit with a blank name. The editing form should retain your changes and explain the error, just like the creation form. Correct the name before continuing.

docs.title: Extract the repeated lookup
docs.text:
show, edit, and update all start with the same product lookup. A before_action lets us run it once before any of those actions.

In app/controllers/products_controller.py, add this import alongside the existing imports:

from flaskteroids.actions import before_action

Add the declaration inside ProductsController, before its existing methods:

class ProductsController(ApplicationController):
    before_action("_set_product", only=["show", "edit", "update"])

    # Keep the existing actions and private methods here.

Replace show, edit, and update with these methods, and add _set_product:

    def show(self):
        pass

    def edit(self):
        pass

    def update(self):
        if self.product.update(**self._product_params()):
            return self.redirect_to(product_path(self.product))
        return self.render("edit", status=422)

    def _set_product(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["id"])

Keep index, new, create, and _product_params unchanged. Empty show and edit actions still render their matching templates; the callback supplies the record first.

Try it: visit a product and edit it again. The behavior should be identical; we have removed duplication without changing the interface.

docs.title: Delete a product
docs.text:
We can browse, create, and edit. The last CRUD operation is deletion.

Add products_path to the existing route-helper import:

from flaskteroids.routes import product_path, products_path

Add this action:

    def destroy(self):
        self.product.destroy()
        return self.redirect_to(products_path(), status=303)

Update the existing before_action call inside ProductsController to include destroy. Replace the call rather than adding a second one:

    before_action("_set_product", only=["show", "edit", "update", "destroy"])

After the Edit link in app/views/products/show.html, add a deletion button:

{{ button_to("Delete", product, method="DELETE") }}

This generates a POST form with a CSRF token and a hidden DELETE override. Deleting data is a state-changing operation, not a GET link. The controller redirects with status 303 so the browser retrieves the catalog afterward.

Try it: create a temporary product, delete it, and confirm that it disappears from the catalog. Keep the original products for the next chapters.

You now have a complete CRUD interface. If you later add callbacks that can reject destruction, handle a False result from destroy() explicitly.

docs.title: The scaffold shortcut
docs.text:
You have built the pieces yourself so you can understand and customize them. For a future resource, a scaffold generates those pieces together. For example, in a separate application:

bin/flask generate scaffold Post title:string content:text
bin/flask db:migrate

Do not generate a Product scaffold over this tutorial: generators may overwrite your work. Next, let's decide who should be allowed to change the catalog.

docs.title: 8. Require login to change products
docs.text:
Right now, anyone can create, edit, or delete products. Stop the server and run:

bin/flask generate authentication
bin/flask db:migrate

The generator adds User and Session models, login/logout and password-reset controllers, templates, mailers, routes, and tests. It also adds an Authentication concern to ApplicationController, making authentication the default for its subclasses. There is no public sign-up form.

Open bin/flask shell and create your own account:

from getpass import getpass

password = getpass("Choose a password: ")
user = User.create(
    email_address="you@example.org",
    password=password,
    password_confirmation=password,
)
assert not user.errors, user.errors.full_messages()
del password
exit()

has_secure_password() hashes the password; the database stores a digest, not its plaintext. Use a real password of your own, and do not put it in source code.

Restart the server and visit http://127.0.0.1:5000/products/new. You should be redirected to the login page at /session/new. Log in with your account.

docs.title: Keep the catalog public
docs.text:
Visitors should still be able to browse products without an account. In app/controllers/products_controller.py, add skip_before_action to the existing actions import:

from flaskteroids.actions import before_action, skip_before_action

Replace the existing callback declaration inside ProductsController with these two class-body calls, keeping its methods unchanged:

    skip_before_action("_require_authentication", only=["index", "show"])
    before_action("_set_product", only=["show", "edit", "update", "destroy"])

The generated Authentication concern provides the is_authenticated() template helper. It resumes the session when needed, including on public pages where _require_authentication is skipped. No extra callback or controller variable is needed.

docs.title: Show login and logout controls
docs.text:
Use the generated singular session resource for logout. Its session_path() destination accepts POST for login and DELETE for logout; button_to renders the browser-safe POST form, hidden DELETE override, and CSRF token. No extra logout endpoint or JavaScript is needed.

In app/views/products/index.html, replace the New product link with:

{% if is_authenticated() %}
  {{ link_to("New product", new_product_path()) }}
  {{ button_to("Log out", session_path(), method="DELETE") }}
{% else %}
  {{ link_to("Log in", new_session_path()) }}
{% endif %}

In app/views/products/show.html, wrap the Edit and Delete controls:

{% if is_authenticated() %}
  {{ link_to("Edit", edit_product_path(product)) }}
  {{ button_to("Delete", product, method="DELETE") }}
{% endif %}

Hiding controls is not access control: the controller callback protects the write actions even if someone sends a request directly. This example has one role: every account can manage the catalog. Ownership checks, permissions, and public registration need additional application rules.

Log out and verify that browsing still works, while /products/new requires login again. Password reset also needs working mail delivery before real users can rely on it.

Checkpoint: guests can browse the catalog, but only signed-in users can create, edit, or delete products. Keep the account you created: we'll use it to manage inventory shortly. We'll add automated checks after building the features.

docs.title: 9. Upload product images
docs.text:
A shopper can browse the catalog, but an image makes a product easier to recognize. Let's add a photo without changing the product's ordinary edit flow. Install the attachment tables and configuration:

bin/flask attachments:install
bin/flask db:migrate

Stop and restart the server after this migration, as with other schema changes.

In app/models/product.py, import has_one_attached alongside validates, then update the declarations inside Product to:

    validates("name", presence=True)
    has_one_attached(
        "featured_image",
        max_size=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_types=["image/png", "image/jpeg"],
    )

The attachment is not an extra column on products: the attachment tables keep track of files and their owning records.

Inside the form_with block in app/views/products/_form.html, before the submit button, add:

<div>
  {{ form.label("featured_image") }}
  {{ form.file_field("featured_image", accept="image/png,image/jpeg") }}
</div>

form_with detects the file field and adds multipart encoding. Permit the upload by replacing _product_params() in ProductsController with:

    def _product_params(self):
        return self.params.expect(product=["name", "description", "featured_image"])

In the body block of app/views/products/show.html, add:

{% if product.featured_image.attached() %}
  <img src="{{ blob_path(product.featured_image) }}" alt="{{ product.name }}">
{% endif %}

Log in, edit a product, and upload a small PNG or JPEG. After saving, its show page should display the image. Reopen Edit and save without selecting another file: the existing image should remain. Files become available after the save commits.

Development uses local disk storage. Signed download links are accessible to anyone who has the link by default, which suits public catalog images but not private documents. Content-type checks are not file scanning. See Attachments for storage services, authorization, request size limits, and cleanup jobs.

docs.title: 10. Notify visitors when products return to stock
docs.text: Our catalog can describe a product and show its image, but it cannot answer a shopper's next question: "Can I get one?" Let's track inventory. If a product sells out, visitors will be able to subscribe to a restock email and unsubscribe later.

docs.title: Track inventory
docs.text:
Stop the server and generate a migration for the existing products table:

bin/flask generate migration AddInventoryCountToProducts inventory_count:integer

Open the new file under db/migrate/versions/. In upgrade(), change only the inventory_count column to add nullable=False and server_default="0":

sa.Column("inventory_count", sa.Integer(), nullable=False, server_default="0")

Keep the rest of the migration unchanged. The default gives existing and new products a count of zero; nullable=False prevents null values. These are inventory-specific choices, not defaults the generator can infer.

Apply it:

bin/flask db:migrate

Replace app/models/product.py with the following, preserving the attachment declaration we added earlier:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_one_attached, validates


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    validates("name", presence=True)
    validates("inventory_count", numericality={"only_integer": True})
    validates("inventory_count", comparison={"greater_than_or_equal_to": 0})
    has_one_attached(
        "featured_image",
        max_size=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_types=["image/png", "image/jpeg"],
    )

The database supplies the default; validations explain invalid user input. Both inventory_count declarations apply: repeated validates calls add checks rather than replacing earlier ones.

Add this field before the submit button in app/views/products/_form.html:

<div>
  {{ form.label("inventory_count") }}
  {{ form.number_field("inventory_count") }}
</div>

Replace _product_params() in ProductsController so edits can include stock:

    def _product_params(self):
        return self.params.expect(
            product=["name", "description", "featured_image", "inventory_count"]
        )

Create app/views/products/_inventory.html:

{% if product.inventory_count > 0 %}
  <p>{{ product.inventory_count }} in stock</p>
{% else %}
  <p>Out of stock</p>
{% endif %}

Include it after the description in app/views/products/show.html:

{% include "products/_inventory.html" %}

Restart the server. Try it: an existing product should say Out of stock. Log in, edit its inventory count to 5, and save: the page should say 5 in stock. Try -1 and check that the form explains the error and keeps the entered value. Finally set the count to 0 so we can build the subscription experience.

docs.title: Remember who wants an email
docs.text:
A product can have many subscribers, and each subscriber belongs to a product. Generate the subscriber model and its migration:

bin/flask generate model Subscriber product:references email:string unsubscribe_token:string

The reference creates product_id and a foreign key. Open the generated CreateSubscribers migration and add this after op.create_table(...) in upgrade():

    op.create_index(
        "ix_subscribers_unsubscribe_token",
        "subscribers",
        ["unsubscribe_token"],
        unique=True,
    )

The generated downgrade() drops the table, including its index. Apply the migration:

bin/flask db:migrate

Replace app/models/subscriber.py with:

from secrets import token_urlsafe

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import before_create, belongs_to, validates


class Subscriber(ApplicationModel):
    belongs_to("product")
    validates("email", presence=True)
    before_create("_assign_unsubscribe_token")

    def _assign_unsubscribe_token(self):
        self.unsubscribe_token = token_urlsafe(32)

A before_create callback assigns a random token before the record is first saved. That token will let someone unsubscribe without an account. Treat it like a credential: do not expose a subscriber list or log the tokens.

In app/models/product.py, add has_many to the existing model import and add has_many("subscribers", dependent="destroy") inside the model class. Deleting a product will now delete its subscriptions too.

Restart the server, then open bin/flask shell:

>>> product = Product.find_by(name="Cotton T-Shirt")
>>> subscriber = Subscriber.create(product=product, email="reader@example.org")
>>> subscriber.product.name
'Cotton T-Shirt'
>>> [person.email for person in product.subscribers]
['reader@example.org']
>>> bool(subscriber.unsubscribe_token)
True

The association connects the objects without manually looking up a foreign-key value. Exit the shell. Next, let's let visitors do this from the product page.

docs.title: Add the subscription form
docs.text:
Create app/controllers/subscribers_controller.py:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.product import Product
from flaskteroids.actions import skip_before_action
from flaskteroids.routes import product_path


class SubscribersController(ApplicationController):
    skip_before_action("_require_authentication")

    def create(self):
        self.product = Product.find(self.params["product_id"])
        self.subscriber = self.product.subscribers.where(
            **self.params.expect(subscriber=["email"])
        ).first_or_create()
        if not self.subscriber.is_persisted():
            return self.render("new", status=422)
        return self.redirect_to(
            product_path(self.product),
            notice="We will email you when it is back in stock.",
        )

Subscriptions are public, unlike editing stock. The email is allowlisted, and the product comes from the URL rather than an editable form field. Looking up an existing subscription through the product's association avoids adding another during ordinary repeat visits. first_or_create() returns the existing record or attempts to save a new one using the scope's email and parent. A rejected save returns its errors and entered values for redisplay. This lookup is not an atomic uniqueness guarantee; a production signup service also needs database constraints, confirmation, and abuse controls.

In config/routes.py, replace the existing route.resources("products") declaration with the nested resource, keeping your other routes:

    route.resources(
        "products",
        nested=lambda child: child.resources("subscribers", only=["create"]),
    )

Product member actions still receive id; subscriber creation receives product_id. Python and templates can both use product_subscribers_path(product).

The nested URL tells the controller which product the visitor wants to follow. Replace app/views/products/_inventory.html with:

{% if product.inventory_count > 0 %}
  <p>{{ product.inventory_count }} in stock</p>
{% else %}
  <p>Out of stock</p>
  <p>Email me when it is available:</p>
  {% call(form) form_with(model=[product, Subscriber.new()]) %}
    {{ form.email_field("email", required=True, placeholder="you@example.org") }}
    {{ form.submit("Notify me") }}
  {% endcall %}
{% endif %}

The final model determines field scope and values, so the email is named subscriber[email] automatically. The parent supplies the nested URL binding; it does not become the field prefix or enable nested-attribute persistence. The controller filters the child with self.params.expect(subscriber=["email"]).

Create app/views/subscribers/new.html for invalid submissions:

{% extends "layouts/application.html" %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>Follow {{ product.name }}</h1>
  <ul class="errors">
    {% for message in subscriber.errors.full_messages() %}
      <li>{{ message }}</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
  {% call(form) form_with(model=[product, subscriber]) %}
    {{ form.email_field("email", required=True) }}
    {{ form.submit("Notify me") }}
  {% endcall %}
  {{ link_to("Back", product_path(product)) }}
{% endblock %}

Our successful redirect sets a flash notice. In app/views/layouts/application.html, add this just after <body>, before the body block:

{% if flash.notice %}<p role="status">{{ flash.notice }}</p>{% endif %}
{% if flash.alert %}<p role="alert">{{ flash.alert }}</p>{% endif %}

Try it: log out, open an out-of-stock product, and subscribe with another email address. You should return to the product and see the confirmation. Subscribe with the same address again: the ordinary repeat request should still show confirmation, not create another record. In a new shell, select the product with product = Product.find_by(name="Cotton T-Shirt"), then check Subscriber.where(product_id=product.id).count().

docs.title: Let subscribers leave
docs.text:
Before sending notifications, let's give recipients a way to stop them. Add these routes inside register in config/routes.py:

    route.get("/unsubscribe/<token>/", to="unsubscribes#show", as_="unsubscribe")
    route.post(
        "/unsubscribe/<token>/", to="unsubscribes#destroy", as_="cancel_subscription"
    )

Create app/controllers/unsubscribes_controller.py:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.models.subscriber import Subscriber
from flaskteroids.actions import skip_before_action


class UnsubscribesController(ApplicationController):
    skip_before_action("_require_authentication")

    def show(self):
        self.subscriber = Subscriber.find_by(unsubscribe_token=self.params["token"])
        if self.subscriber is None:
            return self.redirect_to("/", notice="This subscription is no longer active.")

    def destroy(self):
        subscriber = Subscriber.find_by(unsubscribe_token=self.params["token"])
        if subscriber is not None:
            subscriber.destroy()
        return self.redirect_to("/", notice="You are unsubscribed.")

Create app/views/unsubscribes/show.html:

{% extends "layouts/application.html" %}

{% block body %}
  <h1>Stop following {{ subscriber.product.name }}?</h1>
  {% call(form) form_with(url=url_for("cancel_subscription", token=subscriber.unsubscribe_token)) %}
    {{ form.submit("Unsubscribe") }}
  {% endcall %}
{% endblock %}

Opening an email link displays a confirmation; only submitting its CSRF-protected POST form removes the subscription. Email link scanners therefore do not unsubscribe someone just by following a GET request. Invalid or already-used tokens redirect safely to the catalog.

docs.title: Write the restock email
docs.text:
Generate a mailer:

bin/flask generate mailer Product in_stock

Replace app/mailers/product_mailer.py with:

from app.mailers.application_mailer import ApplicationMailer


class ProductMailer(ApplicationMailer):
    def in_stock(self):
        self.product = self.params["product"]
        self.subscriber = self.params["subscriber"]
        return self.mail(
            to=self.subscriber.email,
            subject=f"{self.product.name} is back in stock",
        )

with_params(...) supplies the mailer's self.params, using the same API as controllers without an HTTP request. Instance variables expose the product and subscriber to templates; queued delivery reloads these saved records.

Email links need absolute URLs: product_url is the absolute counterpart of product_path. The custom unsubscribe endpoint still uses url_for with _external=True.

Replace app/views/product_mailer/in_stock.html with:

<h1>Good news!</h1>
<p>{{ link_to(product.name, product_url(product)) }} is back in stock.</p>
<p>{{ link_to("Unsubscribe", url_for("unsubscribe", token=subscriber.unsubscribe_token, _external=True)) }}</p>

Replace app/views/product_mailer/in_stock.txt with:

Good news! {{ product.name }} is back in stock.
{{ product_url(product) }}

Unsubscribe: {{ url_for("unsubscribe", token=subscriber.unsubscribe_token, _external=True) }}

docs.title: Preview delivery locally
docs.text:
We want to see the message without needing a real mailbox. Create app/mailers/console_delivery.py, an application-owned development adapter:

class ConsoleDeliveryMethod:
    def __init__(self, application, config):
        pass

    def deliver(self, message):
        print(f"To: {message['To']}", flush=True)
        print(f"Subject: {message['Subject']}", flush=True)
        print(message.get_body(preferencelist=("plain",)).get_content(), flush=True)

Replace config/environments/development.py with:

from app.mailers.console_delivery import ConsoleDeliveryMethod


def configure(config):
    config.enable_reloading = True
    config.consider_all_requests_local = True
    config.action_controller.perform_caching = False
    config.attachments.service = "local"
    config["SERVER_NAME"] = "127.0.0.1:5000"
    config.action_mailer.perform_deliveries = True
    config.action_mailer.delivery_method = ConsoleDeliveryMethod
    config.active_job.broker_url = "sqla+sqlite:///storage/jobs_database.db"

SERVER_NAME supplies a host for absolute links even in the shell. This adapter prints mail; it does not send real messages. The development queue uses a local SQLite file, so this example needs no separate broker server.

Restart the web server. Open a new bin/flask shell and preview one email:

from app.mailers.product_mailer import ProductMailer

subscriber = Subscriber.find_by(email="reader@example.org")
product = subscriber.product
ProductMailer.with_params(
    product=product, subscriber=subscriber
).in_stock().deliver_now()

You should see a readable message preview in the shell, with a subject ending in "is back in stock", a product link, and an unsubscribe link. Exit the shell. The action runs immediately; deliver_later() queues its captured template assigns, not self.params. See Mailers for delivery details.

docs.title: Trigger notifications after a restock
docs.text:
Now connect inventory to email. Replace app/models/product.py with:

from app.mailers.product_mailer import ProductMailer
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import (
    after_commit,
    has_many,
    has_one_attached,
    validates,
)


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    validates("name", presence=True)
    validates("inventory_count", numericality={"only_integer": True})
    validates("inventory_count", comparison={"greater_than_or_equal_to": 0})
    has_one_attached(
        "featured_image",
        max_size=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_types=["image/png", "image/jpeg"],
    )
    has_many("subscribers", dependent="destroy")
    after_commit("_notify_subscribers", on="update", if_="_back_in_stock")

    def _back_in_stock(self):
        change = self.saved_change_to_attribute("inventory_count")
        return change is not None and change[0] == 0 and change[1] > 0

    def _notify_subscribers(self):
        for subscriber in self.subscribers:
            ProductMailer.with_params(
                product=self, subscriber=subscriber
            ).in_stock().deliver_later()

saved_change_to_attribute() returns the old and new typed values from the latest successful save, or None when that attribute did not change. A change from zero to a positive count triggers one email per subscriber. An ordinary description edit or a change from 5 to 6 does not send a new batch.

after_commit runs only after the outer transaction commits, so a rollback never enqueues these notifications. The callback can query subscribers normally; the mailer captures each message's recipient and subject when called, while queued template models reload at delivery. If an explicit transaction saves the same product more than once, the condition describes its last successful save, not every intermediate transition. See Models for callbacks, saved changes, and transactions.

docs.title: Watch the complete feature work
docs.text:
Restart the web server to load the model. From store, start a worker in another terminal:

.venv/bin/celery -A jobs worker --loglevel=info

The web process and worker read the same development configuration and local queue. Keep both running for this checkpoint:

  1. Log in and set Cotton T-Shirt's inventory count to 0.
  2. Log out and subscribe from its product page with a second email address.
  3. Log in again, change the inventory count to 5, and save.
  4. Watch the worker terminal: one message per subscribed address should appear.
  5. Change the count from 5 to 6. There should be no new restock email.
  6. Copy an unsubscribe URL from a message into the browser and confirm removal.
  7. Set stock to 0 and then 5 again. That recipient should no longer get an email.

We now have a reason for every piece: inventory drives the page, associations remember interested visitors, callbacks notice a restock, and a mailer and job queue deliver the notification outside the request.

The console adapter is for development only. Real delivery needs SMTP settings and a sender address; production also needs a worker and a suitable shared broker when running multiple instances. Generated production settings read CELERY_BROKER_URL. See Mailers, Background jobs, and Configuration for those settings.

docs.title: 11. Give the store a little polish
docs.text:
The generated layout already includes app/assets/stylesheets/application.css. Replace or extend that file with:

body {
  font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  max-width: 60rem;
  margin: 2rem auto;
  padding: 0 1rem;
}

form div {
  margin: 1rem 0;
}

label {
  display: block;
}

img {
  max-width: 100%;
  height: auto;
}

.errors {
  color: #b91c1c;
}

Refresh a product page to see the change. Development serves source assets directly. Production uses fingerprinted files, built with:

bin/flask assets:precompile

Docker builds run this compilation automatically. Keep the generated output and manifest together; production has no fallback to source files.

The generated layout also loads Turbo from a CDN. Flaskteroids' asset compiler does not install import maps, bundle JavaScript, or compile Sass. See Assets when extending the frontend.

docs.title: 12. Test the store's behavior
docs.text:
We have exercised the store in a browser. Let's turn its important behaviors into repeatable tests: valid products save, guests can subscribe but cannot edit, and restocking emails the right people.

Tests use a separate test environment and database. bin/flask test applies pending migrations and runs pytest-based tests. Framework test classes roll back their database changes between tests. The test mail and queue adapters keep messages in memory, so you do not need the development worker or real SMTP.

docs.title: Give the tests a small catalog
docs.text:
Create test/fixtures/products.yml:

shirt:
  name: T-Shirt
  description: A comfortable cotton shirt.
  inventory_count: 0

Create test/fixtures/subscribers.yml:

reader:
  product: shirt
  email: reader@example.org
  unsubscribe_token: reader-test-token

another:
  product: shirt
  email: another@example.org
  unsubscribe_token: another-test-token

Fixture labels connect subscribers to shirt without hard-coded IDs. These example tokens belong only to the test database; real subscriptions generate random ones. Declare both fixture sets in tests that need the association.

docs.title: Test products and restock notifications
docs.text:
Replace test/models/product_test.py with:

from test.test_helper import ModelTest

import pytest

from app.models.product import Product


class ProductTest(ModelTest):
    fixtures = ["products", "subscribers"]

    def test_save_persists_valid_product(self):
        product = Product.new(name="Socks", description="Warm socks.")

        assert product.save()
        assert Product.find(product.id).name == "Socks"

    def test_save_rejects_blank_name(self):
        product = Product.new(name="")

        assert not product.save()
        assert product.errors
        assert product.id is None

    def test_inventory_rejects_negative_input(self):
        product = Product.new(name="Socks", inventory_count=-1)

        assert not product.save()
        assert product.inventory_count == -1
        assert product.errors

    def test_restock_emails_subscribers(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")

        with self.assert_emails(2), self.perform_enqueued_jobs():
            assert product.update(inventory_count=5)

        assert {message["To"] for message in self.deliveries} == {
            "reader@example.org",
            "another@example.org",
        }

    def test_positive_stock_adjustment_preserves_notification_count(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")
        assert product.update(inventory_count=5)

        with self.assert_emails(0), self.perform_enqueued_jobs():
            assert product.update(inventory_count=6)

    def test_rolled_back_restock_keeps_queue_empty(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")

        with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="Cancel restock"):
            with Product.transaction():
                assert product.update(inventory_count=5)
                assert not self.enqueued_jobs
                raise ValueError("Cancel restock")

        assert not self.enqueued_jobs

The notification test changes stock from zero to five and performs jobs as they are enqueued. It checks the recipients as well as the count. The other cases check that ordinary stock adjustments and rolled-back updates do not produce restock notifications.

Run just these tests:

bin/flask test test/models/product_test.py

You should see them pass without contacting a broker or mail server.

docs.title: Check the actual email
docs.text:
Replace the generated test/mailers/product_mailer_test.py with:

from test.test_helper import MailerTest

from app.mailers.product_mailer import ProductMailer


class ProductMailerTest(MailerTest):
    fixtures = ["products", "subscribers"]

    def test_email_contains_product_and_unsubscribe_links(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")
        subscriber = self.subscribers("reader")

        with self.assert_emails(1):
            ProductMailer.with_params(
                product=product, subscriber=subscriber
            ).in_stock().deliver_now()

        message = self.deliveries[0]
        assert message["To"] == subscriber.email
        assert message["Subject"] == "T-Shirt is back in stock"
        text = message.get_body(preferencelist=("plain",)).get_content()
        assert f"/products/{product.id}" in text
        assert f"/unsubscribe/{subscriber.unsubscribe_token}/" in text

docs.title: Check guest access and subscriptions
docs.text:
Replace test/controllers/products_controller_test.py with:

from test.test_helper import IntegrationTest, get, post

from app.models.subscriber import Subscriber
from flaskteroids.routes import new_product_path, new_session_path, products_path


class ProductsControllerTest(IntegrationTest):
    fixtures = ["products", "subscribers"]

    def test_guest_can_browse_products(self):
        get(products_path())

        self.assert_response("success")

    def test_guest_is_redirected_to_login(self):
        get(new_product_path())

        self.assert_redirected_to(new_session_path())

    def test_guest_can_subscribe_to_product(self):
        product = self.products("shirt")

        with self.assert_difference(Subscriber.count):
            post(
                f"/products/{product.id}/subscribers",
                params={"subscriber": {"email": "new-reader@example.org"}},
            )

        assert Subscriber.find_by(
            product_id=product.id, email="new-reader@example.org"
        )

    def test_unsubscribe_link_requires_confirmation(self):
        subscriber = self.subscribers("reader")
        path = f"/unsubscribe/{subscriber.unsubscribe_token}/"

        with self.assert_difference(Subscriber.count, by=0):
            get(path)
        self.assert_response("success")

        with self.assert_difference(Subscriber.count, by=-1):
            post(path)
        self.assert_redirected_to("/")

The request helpers simulate HTTP without starting a web server. Checking both GET and POST makes the unsubscribe boundary explicit: following the email link is safe; confirming the form removes the subscription.

docs.title: Walk through an edit in a real browser
docs.text:
Create test/system/products_test.py:

from test.test_helper import SystemTest

from app.models.user import User
from flaskteroids.routes import new_product_path


class ProductsTest(SystemTest):
    def setup(self):
        User.create(
            email_address="owner@example.org",
            password="test-password-only",
            password_confirmation="test-password-only",
        )

    def test_owner_creates_and_edits_product(self):
        self.visit(new_product_path())
        self.page.get_by_placeholder("Enter your email address").fill("owner@example.org")
        self.page.locator('input[name="password"]').fill("test-password-only")
        self.click_on("Sign in")
        self.assert_selector("h1", text="New product")

        self.fill_in("Name", with_="Browser hat")
        self.fill_in("Description", with_="A hat created in the browser.")
        self.click_on("Save product")
        self.assert_selector("h1", text="Browser hat")

        self.click_on("Edit")
        self.fill_in("Name", with_="Updated browser hat")
        self.click_on("Save product")
        self.assert_selector("h1", text="Updated browser hat")

The test follows the login flow rather than constructing a session cookie. Its password is fixed test data, not an account used in development or production. Browser tests use Playwright. Install Chromium once, then run the suite:

.venv/bin/playwright install chromium
bin/flask test:system

You should see the browser journey pass. Run all non-browser tests too:

bin/flask test

The generated health and authentication tests should pass alongside the tests we wrote. You now have checks for the whole story, from editing a product to subscribing and delivering its restock email. See Testing for uploads, additional assertions, and running selected tests in parallel.

docs.title: 13. Security and continuous integration
docs.text:
Before deploying, run the complete suite:

bin/flask test
bin/flask test:system

The generated .github/workflows/test.yml provides a starting CI workflow. Review it and keep your application's tests and browser dependencies up to date. Linting or security scanners you choose for your application need their own configuration.

Keep these boundaries in mind:

  • Use self.params.expect() allowlists, even when the browser form looks harmless.
  • Protect write actions on the server, not just their links in templates.
  • Keep CSRF protection enabled; form helpers include the required tokens.
  • Let Jinja and helpers escape user input. Never mark product descriptions safe merely to display formatting.
  • Keep master keys, passwords, database URLs, and SMTP credentials out of Git.
  • Do not expose the debug server to production traffic.
  • Configure HTTPS, upload limits, access policies, and backups for your deployment.

docs.title: 14. Prepare for production
docs.text:
Flaskteroids generates a Dockerfile and deployment scripts. Start by reading your app's deploy/README.md, which contains the commands matching your generated application. You will need to choose and configure your own hosting platform.

For a local production-mode Docker check, commit your application lockfile and build an image:

docker build -t store .
docker volume create store-storage

Supply FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY at runtime using your secret manager. For a local check only, read the generated key into your shell and forward it to Docker:

export FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY="$(tr -d '\n' < config/master.key)"
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
  --env FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY \
  --volume store-storage:/app/storage \
  store

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. This is a separate production database, so it will not contain the development products or account you created earlier. Stop the container with Ctrl-C when finished and unset the key:

unset FLASKTEROIDS_MASTER_KEY

The default web startup prepares the production database before launching Gunicorn. The volume keeps SQLite data and local uploads across container restarts. The image runs unprivileged; host bind mounts must be writable by its application user.

For a real deployment:

  1. Provide the matching credentials key and environment settings through your hosting platform's secret management.
  2. Configure your database and install its driver if using PostgreSQL or MySQL.
  3. Coordinate migrations once per release when running multiple instances; do not use each web instance as migration coordination.
  4. Configure SMTP and a sender address for real mail, your canonical host via SERVER_NAME for email links, external storage if needed, and a Celery broker and worker. The tutorial's console adapter is only enabled in development.
  5. Put the application behind HTTPS and arrange persistent storage and backups.
  6. Create an initial user through an application shell in the production environment, using your host's execution facility and the account creation code from this guide. Do not add credentials to the image or Git.

See Configuration and your generated deployment guide for release commands and service settings. The Docker check above is not a complete internet-facing deployment recipe.

docs.title: 15. Where to go next
docs.text:
You started with an empty application and built a working store: visitors browse products, owners manage stock and images, and subscribers hear when a product returns. Tests now check the behavior that makes those features work together.

Next, try expanding it:

  • Add product categories with another model and association.
  • Add pagination and filtering to the catalog.
  • Confirm subscription addresses before enabling notifications for real visitors.
  • Write a browser test for the complete subscribe-and-unsubscribe journey.
  • Return JSON alongside HTML using controller content negotiation.

Explore the focused guides as you go:

  • Models: queries, transactions, associations, and callbacks.
  • Controllers and Routing.
  • Views and Forms.
  • Attachments, Mailers, and Background jobs.
  • Testing, Configuration, and CLI.

A new app is ready to run. When you check out an existing project—or create one with --skip-install—run bin/setup to install its dependencies and prepare the database.

Next, explore Configuration to choose settings for each environment, or Assets to add styles and images.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Tests grow alongside your application. Generators give you starting tests for new features, and your new app includes a health check to get you going.

Run model, controller, job, and mailer tests as you work:

bin/flask test

Use browser tests to check the journey a person takes through your app:

bin/flask test:system

Both commands use pytest, so you can focus on one file or run tests in parallel:

bin/flask test -n auto
bin/flask test test/controllers/posts_controller_test.py

The commands use your test environment and apply pending migrations. Tests that inherit from Flaskteroids test classes roll back their database changes, keeping each test independent.

For upload tests, put example files in test/fixtures/files and use fixture_file_upload('avatar.png'). Uploads use temporary storage, leaving your real files untouched. See Attachments for examples.

docs.title: Test types
docs.text:
from test.test_helper import (
    IntegrationTest,
    JobTest,
    MailerTest,
    ModelTest,
    SystemTest,
)

Generated tests use files ending in _test.py and classes ending in Test.

docs.title: Fixtures
docs.text:
Fixtures live under test/fixtures:

# test/fixtures/posts.yml
one:
  title: First post
  content: First post content

two:
  title: Second post
  content: Second post content

Declare and access them from a test:

class PostTest(ModelTest):
    fixtures = ["posts"]

    def setup(self):
        self.post = self.posts("one")

Each test gets its declared fixtures, and its changes are rolled back afterward. Use fixture labels rather than hard-coded IDs; generated IDs may have gaps.

docs.title: Integration tests
docs.text:
from test.test_helper import IntegrationTest, get, post
from app.models.post import Post
from flaskteroids.routes import post_url, posts_url


class PostsControllerTest(IntegrationTest):
    fixtures = ["posts"]

    def test_should_get_index(self):
        get(posts_url())
        self.assert_response("success")

    def test_should_create_post(self):
        with self.assert_difference(Post.count):
            post(
                posts_url(),
                params={"post": {"title": "New post", "content": "Content"}},
            )

        self.assert_redirected_to(post_url(Post.last()))

Available request functions are get, post, patch, put, and delete.

docs.title: Jobs and mail
docs.text:
The test environment uses in-memory job and mail adapters:

with self.assert_enqueued_with(job=PublishPostJob, args=[post]):
    PublishPostJob.perform_later(post)

with self.perform_enqueued_jobs():
    PublishPostJob.perform_later(post)

with self.assert_emails(1):
    PostsMailer.published(post).deliver_now()

No broker or SMTP server is required.

docs.title: System tests
docs.text:
System tests use Playwright through helpers such as visit and assert_selector:

class PostsTest(SystemTest):
    def test_visiting_posts(self):
        self.visit(posts_path())
        self.assert_selector("h1", text="Posts")

Flaskteroids includes the Playwright Python package, but not its browser binaries. Install Chromium before your first system test run:

.venv/bin/playwright install chromium

docs.title: Controllers
docs.text:
Controllers handle HTTP requests. Each action is a method on a controller class. Unless an action prepares a response, Flaskteroids renders its matching template with the controller's instance variables. Native Flask response return values, including empty strings and dictionaries, remain supported.

# app/controllers/posts_controller.py
from flaskteroids.controller import ActionController
from app.models.post import Post

class PostsController(ActionController):
    def index(self):
        self.posts = Post.all()
        # Implicitly renders app/views/posts/index.html and
        # makes self.posts available in the template.

    def show(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params["id"])
        # Implicitly renders app/views/posts/show.html and
        # makes self.post available in the template.

Read request input from self.params; templates access the same mapping as params. Use self.params.expect(...) to allowlist model attributes.

docs.title: Controller callbacks
docs.text:
Import declaration functions explicitly. They follow the same class-body declaration contracts as models and mailers, including inheritance through ordinary mixins.

Call before_action inside the controller class to run code before an action. Use it to load records shared by several actions or check authentication:

from flaskteroids.actions import before_action
from flaskteroids.controller import ActionController
from app.models.post import Post


class PostsController(ActionController):
    before_action("_set_post", only=["show", "edit", "update", "destroy"])

    def show(self):
        # self.post is already set by the callback
        pass

    def _set_post(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params["id"])

docs.title: Inherited actions
docs.text: Children inherit actions and callback declarations. Callbacks without only also cover actions the child adds. Calling super().action() runs the parent action and its callbacks. The same rules apply to mailers.

docs.title: Around and after callbacks
docs.text:
around_action methods are generators. Code before yield runs before the action; code after it runs during cleanup:

from time import monotonic
from flask import current_app
from flaskteroids.actions import around_action


class PostsController(ActionController):
    around_action("_log_duration")

    def index(self):
        self.posts = Post.all()

    def _log_duration(self):
        started = monotonic()
        yield
        current_app.logger.info("Action duration: %.3fs", monotonic() - started)

The callback chain follows these rules:

  • Before callbacks run in declaration order. Preparing a response stops the chain, even without a return value. Returning a response also skips the action, around callbacks, and after callbacks.
  • Around callbacks enter in declaration order and unwind in reverse order. Entered generators are resumed and closed even if the action or a later callback's setup raises. Cleanup resumes the generator normally, rather than throwing the action exception into it.
  • An around generator that returns before reaching yield skips the action, later around callbacks, and after callbacks. Its return value is used as the response. Returning None leaves implicit template rendering in place. Previously entered generators still unwind.
  • Around generators must yield exactly once when they run the action. A second yield raises ProgrammerError and closes the generator.
  • Implicit rendering happens before around cleanup and after callbacks. After callbacks run in declaration order only after the action and cleanup succeed; they can edit self.response, but cannot prepare a second response.

A cleanup failure does not prevent other entered generators from unwinding. If an action or setup exception is already propagating, it remains the exception raised to the caller. Secondary cleanup failures are logged and added to its exception notes. Otherwise, the first cleanup exception is raised and any later cleanup failures are logged and added as notes to it.

docs.title: Rendering responses
docs.text:
self.render("new", status=422) renders a template; self.render() selects the current action. Use self.render(json=value, status=200) for JSON. Status values can be integers or HTTPStatus members.

self.response is available for headers and status before preparing a body; metadata changes do not set self.performed. Pending metadata carries into the response unless explicitly replaced.

Rendering sets self.performed but does not stop execution. Use return self.render(...) when the action should exit immediately. Preparing a second response raises DoubleRenderError from flaskteroids.exceptions.

Template/helper render(...) remains a partial renderer, not a controller response.

Supported payloads include dictionaries, lists, strings, numbers, booleans, and None. Empty dictionaries, lists, and strings remain JSON values; None becomes JSON null. Tuples become JSON arrays.

Models, queries, and other objects with a callable __json__() use that protocol, including when nested inside dictionaries, lists, or tuples. Values returned by __json__() are processed recursively too. Other values are passed to Flask's JSON provider, preserving its supported types and custom serialization.

self.render(json={"posts": Post.all(), "featured": post})

Model errors serialize as the list returned by errors.full_messages(), including [] when there are no errors:

return self.render(json=post.errors, status=422)
# JSON body on validation failure: ["Field title is blank"]

Generated scaffold create and update actions use this response for JSON validation failures. See model serialization for column selection and authentication-field filtering.

docs.title: Redirects and empty responses
docs.text:
self.redirect_to(product_path(product), notice="Saved") prepares a redirect; use status=303 or alert=... when needed. self.head(204) prepares an empty response and accepts a headers dictionary.

Both participate in the same response tracking as render and respond_to. They do not stop action execution; return their result to exit early. In a before callback, preparing a response halts the chain without needing a return.

docs.title: Controller helpers
docs.text:
Presentation methods in app/helpers/*_helper.py are automatically available to views. Use helper(...) to include additional helper classes when automatic inclusion is restricted. These methods execute on the view context, not the controller.

Call helper_method inside the controller class to expose a private method as a callable in templates, layouts, and partials:

from flaskteroids.controller import helper_method


class PostsController(ApplicationController):
    helper_method("_display_name")

    def _display_name(self, post):
        return post.title or "Untitled"

{{ display_name(post) }}

By default, the template name drops the method's leading underscore. Pass name="another_name" to choose a different name. Helpers are inherited, use the current controller instance, and remain private methods rather than routable actions. Unregistered private methods are not exposed. Return ordinary strings for text that should be HTML-escaped.

Mailers support the same declaration via flaskteroids.mailer.helper_method; those helpers delegate to the mailer's own state, not a request controller. See mailer helper methods.

The authentication generator uses this mechanism to expose is_authenticated(). The helper resumes the session on demand, so public pages can show login/logout controls without a separate authentication-status callback. Calling the helper does not require login; _require_authentication enforces access control.

docs.title: Content negotiation
docs.text:
self.respond_to(...) selects an offered HTML or JSON handler using the Accept header (HTML when absent); a .json URL suffix takes precedence. Unsupported formats produce 406. Selected responses are recorded on the controller, so returning the result is optional. HTML handlers may leave template rendering implicit; JSON handlers must render or return a response.

from flaskteroids.controller import ActionController
from app.models.post import Post

class PostsController(ActionController):
    def index(self):
        self.posts = Post.all()
        self.respond_to(
            html=lambda: self.render('index'),
            json=lambda: self.render(json=self.posts)
        )

docs.title: Rate limits
docs.text:
Use the rate_limit declaration to restrict requests to a controller or action. This example allows five requests within 60 seconds:

from flaskteroids.controller import ActionController
from flaskteroids.rate_limit import rate_limit


class MyController(ActionController):
    rate_limit(to=5, within=60)

    def index(self):
        pass

Limits count requests by client IP by default. Each application has separate counters. By default, exceeding a limit returns 429. Pass with_="_rate_limit_exceeded" to use a controller method as the handler.

docs.title: Default cache
docs.text:
