Use flaskteroids.cache.store(key, value, ttl=seconds), fetch(key), and increment(key, ttl=seconds). fetch returns cache.MISSING for missing or expired entries. Incrementing resets the expiry time.

The default cache stores values in memory, separately for each application. Calls outside an application context use a separate cache. Values are not shared between worker processes.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text: Define routes in config/routes.py. Its register function receives a router. Actions use "controller#action": products#show calls ProductsController.show from app/controllers.

docs.title: Individual routes
docs.text:
def register(route):
    route.root(to="products#index")
    route.get("/about", to="pages#about", as_="about")
    route.post("/login", to="sessions#create")
    route.put("/products/<int:id>", to="products#update")
    route.patch("/products/<int:id>", to="products#update")
    route.delete("/products/<int:id>", to="products#destroy")

Use Flask/Werkzeug converter syntax for typed bindings. A root route is optional; without one, Flaskteroids displays its welcome page. Explicit individual paths keep the slash spelling you declare.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
def register(route):
    route.resources("products")
Method Path Action Public path helper GET /products index products_path() POST /products create products_path() GET /products/new new new_product_path() GET /products/<int:id> show product_path(product) GET /products/<int:id>/edit edit edit_product_path(product) PUT/PATCH /products/<int:id> update product_path(product) DELETE /products/<int:id> destroy product_path(product)

Collection and member helpers name destinations, not individual actions. HTTP methods distinguish create from index, and update/destroy from show. Resource paths are generated without trailing slashes. Requests with or without a trailing slash reach the same action, including .json/ requests.

Limit actions with only; an empty list generates no resource actions:

route.resources("products", only=["create", "update", "destroy"])

The collection/member helpers remain available without index/show. Unsupported operations on framework routes return 404; they do not fall back to another verb.

docs.title: Uncountable resources
docs.text:
Uncountable names distinguish collection and member helpers with _index:

route.resources("fish")

fish_index_path()  # /fish
fish_path(fish)    # /fish/1
new_fish_path()    # /fish/new

Model-backed forms and buttons use these same names, including nested resources.

docs.title: Singular resources
docs.text:
A singular resource has no member ID:

route.resource("session", only=["new", "create", "destroy"])

This provides new_session_path() at /session/new and session_path() at /session. POST creates a session; DELETE destroys it. The controller remains plural: SessionsController. A default singular resource additionally provides show, edit, and PUT/PATCH update, but never index.

docs.title: Nested resources
docs.text:
route.resources(
    "products",
    nested=lambda child: child.resources("subscribers"),
)

The parent's own member routes still receive id. A subscriber collection receives product_id; a subscriber member receives both product_id and its own id.

products_path()                              # /products
product_path(product)                        # /products/1
product_subscribers_path(product)            # /products/1/subscribers
product_subscriber_path(product, subscriber) # /products/1/subscribers/2
new_product_subscriber_path(product)         # /products/1/subscribers/new
edit_product_subscriber_path(product, subscriber)
# /products/1/subscribers/2/edit

Multiple levels retain each ancestor's identity. To declare siblings, concatenate or unpack the returned route lists:

route.resources("products", nested=lambda child: [
    *child.resources("subscribers"),
    *child.resources("reviews"),
])

docs.title: Custom parameters
docs.text:
route.resources(
    "products", param="slug",
    nested=lambda child: child.resources("subscribers"),
)

The parent receives slug; the child receives product_slug plus its own id. param="int:sku" instead supplies integer sku and product_sku bindings. Path bindings take precedence over query parameters and form fields. Changing a route parameter does not guess an attribute on a model. Pass explicit identifiers or intentionally override the model's public to_param():

product_path("cotton-shirt")
product_subscriber_path(product_slug="cotton-shirt", id=2)

class Product(ApplicationModel):
    def to_param(self):
        return self.slug if self.is_persisted() else None

The default to_param() returns a persisted record's ID as a string; unsaved records have no member identity. Model-backed forms/buttons for new records use collection destinations instead.

docs.title: Helpers in Python and templates
docs.text:
from flaskteroids.routes import product_path, product_url

product_path(product)               # /products/1
product_path(id=1, page=2)           # /products/1?page=2
product_url(product)                # https://example.test/products/1

The same helpers are available directly in Jinja:

{{ link_to(product.name, product_path(product)) }}

Every _path helper has an absolute _url counterpart. Helpers resolve against the active application, including its script prefix; they do not query records or obtain missing bindings from the current request. Missing bindings raise ValueError; extra positional or duplicate bindings raise TypeError. Ambiguous route/helper declarations and template-global collisions are configuration errors.

Outside a request, use an application context and configure Flask's SERVER_NAME and, where needed, APPLICATION_ROOT and PREFERRED_URL_SCHEME. Explicit callers control query values; do not forward unfiltered request parameters to URL helpers. Native Flask url_for remains available for advanced endpoint-based routing.

An individual route's as_ declares its public helper name:

route.get("/dashboard", to="products#index", as_="dashboard")
# dashboard_path(), dashboard_url()

docs.title: JSON destinations
docs.text:
Use format suffixes, not separate action helpers:

products_path(format="json")        # /products.json
product_path(product, format="json") # /products/1.json

CRUD actions dispatch to the same controller actions as their HTML paths. A controller's self.respond_to(...) selects JSON from a .json suffix or the Accept header. Only JSON format generation is currently supported.

docs.title: HTML method overrides
docs.text:
Browsers submit GET or POST forms. form_with and button_to render PUT/PATCH/DELETE as POST plus a hidden _method and a CSRF token:

{{ button_to("Log out", session_path(), method="DELETE") }}

Use the helpers rather than building hidden fields yourself. An overridden DELETE has the same routing and CSRF protection as an actual DELETE request. Overrides apply to all routes in the application, including native Flask routes; request.method reports the effective method.

For manual requests, only POST can be overridden. The _method form field takes precedence over X-HTTP-Method-Override; query parameters cannot change the method. Unsupported values leave the request as POST.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Flaskteroids models are SQLAlchemy-mapped application objects with Rails-like querying, validation, and persistence methods. Columns come from a generated snapshot of the migrated database; behavior and association declarations stay in model files. There is no separate mapped row hidden behind a model.

docs.title: Define models and migrate
docs.text:
All application models inherit an abstract application base:

# app/models/application_model.py
from flaskteroids.model import Model

class ApplicationModel(Model):
    __abstract__ = True

# app/models/author.py
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_many, validates


class Author(ApplicationModel):
    has_many("posts", dependent="destroy")
    validates("name", presence=True)

    def greeting(self):
        return f"Hello, {self.name}"

# app/models/post.py
from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import belongs_to, validates


class Post(ApplicationModel):
    belongs_to("author")
    validates("title", presence=True)

Create the tables through migrations:

flask generate model Author name:string
flask generate model Post title:string author:references
flask db:prepare

Model/scaffold generators write migrations and behavioral model files. Successful db:migrate, db:prepare, and db:rollback regenerate db/schema.py from the selected database. Commit it, but do not edit it manually. Use flask db:schema:dump to refresh it independently. See CLI.

The snapshot lives alongside migrations in db/, matching Rails conventions. For an existing app with app/schema.py, run flask db:schema:dump, remove the old snapshot, and restart servers and workers. No database changes are needed.

The snapshot contains metadata for tables, columns, keys, constraints, indexes, and server defaults, including tables without a behavioral model. It contains no model behavior, validators, or relationship choices. Post conventionally maps to posts; a model may set __table_name__ = "legacy_posts" for another table.

docs.title: Class-body declarations
docs.text:
Import declaration functions explicitly and call them inside the class body. Aliases and module-qualified imports work normally. Repeated declarations accumulate in source order: several validates(...) calls may validate the same attribute. Association names must remain unique.

Declarations are collected, not bound immediately. Callbacks may name methods defined later in the class, and associations need not resolve during import. Abstract model bases, ordinary Python mixins, and Concern classes may contribute declarations. Each receiving class binds its own configuration; shared ancestors are visited once, base-first in left-to-right order, without mutating parents or siblings. Controllers and mailers use the same declaration mechanism.

Call declarations directly in a class body. A class-body for loop is supported; comprehensions, module-level calls, ordinary helper functions, and runtime methods raise ProgrammerError rather than silently losing declarations. Every direct factory call registers, even if its return value is assigned or passed elsewhere.

For a reusable declaration helper, use @declaration. Its factory returns a binding callable accepting the receiving class, and may compose other declaration factories without registering their inner calls separately:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids import declaration
from flaskteroids.model import validates


@declaration
def required(field):
    return validates(field, presence=True)


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    required("name")
    required("sku")

docs.title: Lazy mapping and normal startup
docs.text:
Importing a model only collects its class-body declarations. It does not require a snapshot or connect to the database. Mapping happens when needed: constructing a record, using the query facade, or accessing a mapped expression such as Post.title.

Consequently, ordinary application startup and migration commands work before a new model has a table in the snapshot. They use the same initialization path; initializers are not skipped. An initializer that actually uses an unavailable model still fails with migration guidance.

The mapper reads the snapshot, not the live database. Restart servers and workers after migration. Do not reload schema files or alter published mappings in place. Abstract behavior bases need no table. Concrete model inheritance, duplicate model names within an application model set, and columns that shadow model APIs are rejected. Different model sets have isolated registries; matching schemas can use the same mapped classes with separate engines/sessions.

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
post = Post.find(1)                      # Raises RecordNotFoundException if absent
post = Post.find_by(title="First")       # Returns None if absent
posts = Post.all()                      # A lazy query
posts = Post.where(title="First")       # A filtered lazy query
records = list(posts)                   # Execute and obtain a list of Post objects
posts = Post.where(Post.title.ilike("a%"))
page = posts.order(title="asc").limit(20).offset(40)
count = page.count()
first = page.first()
last = page.last()

Queries are lazy and immutable. Chain or assign the returned query; a call to query.where(...) does not change the original query. all() always returns a lazy query, including when called on an existing scope; it never executes SQL. Iterating a query loads its selected records. Use list(query) when you need a list. Queries are reusable; each iteration executes again rather than caching results. Default ordering is ascending primary key; order() also accepts native SQLAlchemy ordering expressions. Limits and offsets must be nonnegative or None. count() respects the selected scope/page. first() returns one record or None; last() materializes the selected scope to honor custom ordering and pagination.

Use eager loading to avoid per-row relationship queries:

posts = Post.includes("author")
authors = Author.includes("posts.author")
records = list(posts)

includes() accepts dotted relationship paths and uses native select-in loaders. Unknown relationships raise AttributeError; malformed paths raise ValueError. For complex queries, use query.statement, query.options(...), or native SQLAlchemy.

docs.title: Assignment, validation, and persistence
docs.text:
post = Post.new(title="First", author=author)
if post.save():
    identifier = post.id
else:
    messages = post.errors.full_messages()

post = Post.create(title="", author=author)  # Returns the invalid, unsaved object
assert post.errors
assert post.update(title="Fixed")

Scalar assignments are staged on the mapped object. Reads expose entered values, but SQLAlchemy's published state is unchanged until a successful save. Invalid updates retain their input/errors without being flushed by another object's save or a later commit. This also applies to valid edits never explicitly saved, and to edits made after an earlier save.

A standalone save() validates, flushes, and commits before returning. create() and update() use that same boundary. Associated rows persisted by the save share its transaction. Failure or a halted callback rolls back a standalone operation; earlier successful standalone saves remain committed.

Use an explicit transaction to group operations:

with Author.transaction():
    author = Author.create(name="Ada")
    post = Post.create(title="First", author=author)
    if post.errors:
        raise ValueError("Post is invalid")
# Both writes commit here; an escaping exception rolls both back.

Saves inside an explicit transaction join it without committing. A False return does not abort that outer transaction; raise an exception when the group must fail together. Nested Model.transaction() blocks also join by default. Use Model.transaction(requires_new=True) for a savepoint, catching failures outside that inner block if the outer operation should continue. After-commit callbacks wait for the outer commit, not savepoint release. Transactions are shared across models in the same application, not scoped to the class naming the block.

save(validate=False) explicitly bypasses validation. Database constraints remain authoritative: integrity errors propagate rather than becoming validation errors. Standalone failures clean up their transaction. If a database exception is caught inside an explicit block, recover/roll back that transaction before further writes. A preceding query does not turn a standalone save into an explicit transaction.

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import validates


class Product(ApplicationModel):
    validates("title", presence=True, length={"minimum": 3, "maximum": 100})
    validates("quantity", numericality={"only_integer": True})
    validates("quantity", comparison={"greater_than_or_equal_to": 0})
    validates("email", confirmation=True)

confirmation=True makes a writable confirmation field available. Validators run in declaration order. errors is truthy when populated and exposes count, full_messages(), and JSON full-message lists. is_valid() runs validation without publishing input. Types/casting do not replace explicit user-facing validation.

Model assignment casts supported scalar types and retains original input through read_attribute_before_type_cast(name) and attributes_before_type_cast. Numericality checks raw input rather than trusting a permissive numeric cast. Use numericality={"allow_none": True} for optional numbers; this skips None, not blank strings. Model-backed forms redisplay that input after failed validation; see Fields and Forms.

reload() refreshes published state and discards staged scalar input/errors. discard_changes() only discards staged scalars. Native refresh/expiration does not by itself clear the staging dictionary.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Put persistent defaults in migrations. Simple SQL literal server defaults are available on new objects without querying the database. SQL functions, computed columns, and generated identities remain server-owned and populate on flush. Explicit None is not mistaken for a request to reuse a server default; JSON retains its native JSON-null behavior. As a framework convention, save() maintains declared created_at/updated_at attributes itself; native writes do not implicitly run that timestamp lifecycle.

Python default functions are not recoverable from a database snapshot. Implement application-side defaults explicitly in behavior/callbacks, rather than writing Column.default definitions or editing the generated snapshot.

docs.title: Association declarations
docs.text:
Call association declarations directly inside the model class:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import belongs_to, has_many, has_one


class Post(ApplicationModel):
    belongs_to("author", class_name="User", foreign_key="author_id")
    has_many("comments", dependent="destroy")
    has_one("preview", class_name="Preview", foreign_key="post_id")

The helpers translate into SQLAlchemy relationships before mapping. Class names and foreign keys are inferred conventionally; the shown positional/keyword options remain available. belongs_to() requires its target by default; use optional=True when absence is allowed. inverse_of="posts" selects an explicit inverse when conventions would be ambiguous. The helpers require single-column primary keys; use native relationships for more complex joins.

post.author = author
assert post in author.posts
post.save()

post = Post.create(title="Next", author=author)

Declared has_many associations expose a collection API backed by SQLAlchemy's own collection storage and identity map. Assignment, append/remove, iteration, and native eager loaders still work. Scoped queries do not load the whole collection:

post = author.posts.create(title="Next")
post = author.posts.where(title="Next").first_or_create()
author.posts.where(title="Next").count()

create() saves through the framework and returns the record, including errors and entered values on validation failure. first_or_create() returns the first matching record or creates one; keyword equality filters supply creation values. Additional creation attributes are used only when no record matches. SQL expressions filter queries but are not inferred as creation attributes. The association's parent is authoritative even if attributes contain another parent or foreign key. Creating through an association requires a saved parent; author.posts.new(...) can build an unsaved graph instead. Post.create(author=author, ...) remains supported. Related new framework objects are validated before their staged scalars are published by a framework save.

These find-then-create operations are not atomic uniqueness guarantees. Use a database unique constraint where concurrent duplicate creation must be rejected. Native relationship() declarations retain their native collection API.

Relationship mutations are not scalar staging: they have native unit-of-work semantics. A failed scalar validation does not undo a prior collection edit. When abandoning an invalid transient child, remove it from the collection; do not leave an unpublished new object pending in the session. For coherent inverse updates, assign the relationship itself; raw foreign-key edits may require reloading cached relationships, just as with native SQLAlchemy.

docs.title: Deletion
docs.text:
record.destroy() runs framework destroy callbacks and commits a standalone deletion before returning. Like save(), it joins an explicit transaction when one is open. dependent="destroy" calls related records' framework destroy() methods, including their callbacks and attachment cleanup, in the same boundary. A halted standalone destruction returns False and rolls back earlier dependent deletions. Inside an explicit transaction, raise on rejection when the whole group must roll back.

Native session.delete() and ORM/database cascades do not automatically run framework child destroy() callbacks. Native relationship() options are an escape hatch, but must not be confused with the helper's callback-aware contract. Database ON DELETE choices belong in migrations.

docs.title: Native SQLAlchemy and transactions
docs.text:
from sqlalchemy import inspect, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload
from flaskteroids.db import session

Author.prepare()  # Explicit, database-free mapping for bare native class APIs
mapper = inspect(Author)
author = session.get(Author, 1)
authors = session.scalars(select(Author).options(selectinload(Author.posts))).all()
assert Author.find(author.id) is author

Facade and native queries return the same objects within a session. Mapped columns and relationships are real SQLAlchemy attributes. Staged scalar values are the intentional boundary: SQLAlchemy history and SQL predicates describe published state, not record.changes. read_published_attribute(name) bypasses staged input.

Native callers can explicitly publish without validation or framework callbacks:

post = Post(title="Native", author=author).apply_changes()
session.add(post)
session.flush()

Directly adding a new record with unpublished staged input is rejected at flush, rather than silently inserting null/default data. Native/bulk operations bypass framework validations and operation callbacks. In-place mutable values follow native SQLAlchemy tracking; use scalar reassignment when you want staged edits.

Sessions are app-context-local, with autoflush disabled and committed attributes retained. There is no automatic request-wide transaction. An exception or HTTP error after a successful standalone save does not undo its commit. Context teardown rolls back unfinished work and closes the session; it never commits native writes.

from flaskteroids.db import transaction exposes the same transaction context as Model.transaction(). Native with session.begin(): blocks are also respected; use the framework context when a previous read has already implicitly opened a SQLAlchemy transaction. Native writes require an explicit transaction or an explicit session.commit(). A framework save flushes the session's published work, including native pending changes, so use explicit boundaries when mixing the two APIs. Caller-created sessions are caller-owned.

docs.title: Callbacks and authentication
docs.text:
Call before_validation(...), before_save(...), and other callback declarations inside the model class. Supported operation callbacks include before/after validation; before/around/after save, create, update, and destroy; after initialize/find; and after commit/rollback. Around callbacks are generators that yield once. Before callbacks returning False halt their operation. Callback bodies can update staged scalar attributes.

Load callbacks run when an object is actually hydrated, not on every query that returns an already-loaded identity. After-find runs before after-initialize on hydration. Commit/rollback callbacks are queued by successful framework operations and are transaction-scoped; after-commit runs only after the outer commit, not a flush/savepoint. Commit callbacks can query associations and use the ordinary framework persistence API in a new transaction, with the same session identity map. Exceptions propagate, but cannot undo the transaction already committed. Native and bulk writes do not imply these framework hooks.

docs.title: Saved changes
docs.text:
After a successful framework save, record.saved_changes maps changed scalar attribute names to (old_value, new_value) tuples. Values are typed and include database-assigned IDs/defaults. record.saved_change_to_attribute(name) returns that tuple or None; record.attribute_before_last_save(name) returns the old value, or the published value when unchanged. These APIs are available in after_save and after_commit callbacks without inspecting SQLAlchemy history:

class Product(ApplicationModel):
    after_commit("_notify_subscribers", on="update", if_="_back_in_stock")

    def _back_in_stock(self):
        change = self.saved_change_to_attribute("inventory_count")
        return change is not None and change[0] == 0 and change[1] > 0

    def _notify_subscribers(self):
        for subscriber in self.subscribers:
            ProductMailer.with_params(
                product=self, subscriber=subscriber
            ).in_stock().deliver_later()

Saved changes describe the latest successful save, not pending assignments or a transaction-wide diff. Failed validations preserve that history; a successful unchanged save replaces it. A rollback clears the rolled-back history, and reload() clears it too. When a record is saved repeatedly in one transaction, the commit callback sees its last successful save in that transaction. Rolled-back savepoints do not replace an outer save's commit history. Native publication and bulk writes do not produce framework saved-change history.

Use PasswordAuthenticator and call has_secure_password() inside the model class for password behavior; a custom field name such as has_secure_password("passcode") is supported. Authentication/reset-token checks use published digests, so a failed staged password edit does not invalidate persisted credentials. Passwords, digests, confirmations, and reset tokens are excluded from default JSON/form data. Explicit raw-input APIs remain sensitive; do not log them. Attachments retain their post-commit upload and rollback semantics; see Attachments.

docs.title: Temporary attributes and serialization
docs.text:
Unknown public assignments raise AttributeError. Declare a class default or a property with a setter for transient values, or use a private cache name. Initialize mutable caches per instance. Transients are not automatically saved or serialized; ordinary identity-map lookups return the same instance and its transient state. Framework methods and metadata cannot be replaced through assignment.

Default JSON contains mapped scalar attributes, including staged values, excluding authentication secrets and virtual fields. Override __json__() to define an application-specific response, or add names to _serialization_exclude as a set. Forms obtain values independently of that response representation. Dynamic mapped fields are not generally inferred by ordinary Python editors/type checkers.

docs.title: Assets
docs.text:
Flaskteroids uses Flask's built-in static endpoint at /assets/:

Environment Served directory Development/test app/assets — source files, no build required Other environments public/assets — fingerprinted build output

Flask handles delivery, MIME types, ETags, conditional requests, HEAD, and ranges. Directory structure is preserved in URLs.

docs.title: Helpers
docs.text:
Generated layouts already link app/assets/stylesheets/application.css:

{{ stylesheet_link_tag("application", **{"data-turbo-track": "reload"}) }}
<img src="{{ asset_path("logo.png") }}" alt="Logo">

Helpers are also available from flaskteroids.helpers. stylesheet_link_tag appends .css, accepts multiple names and escaped HTML attributes, and returns trusted markup.

Names are relative to the source root, such as stylesheets/application.css. Short names search immediate subdirectories: application.css and logo.png resolve into stylesheets/ and images/. Ambiguous names raise AssetError; use directory-qualified names to disambiguate.

Helpers generate source URLs in development and manifest-resolved URLs in production. Standard url_for("static", filename=...) still works but does not resolve fingerprints.

docs.title: CSS references
docs.text:
Use ordinary file-relative paths. In stylesheets/application.css:

@import "themes/base.css";
.hero { background-image: url("../images/logo.png"); }
@font-face { font-family: Demo; src: url("../fonts/demo.woff2"); }

All non-hidden asset subdirectories, including fonts/, are included. Compilation rewrites local URLs/imports to fingerprinted files, preserving queries/fragments. Image/font changes also fingerprint dependent stylesheets. Missing references and CSS cycles fail before replacing the previous manifest.

The dependency-free rewriter supports standard quoted/unquoted url(...), quoted @import, and normal CSS escapes in UTF-8 files. Comments, ordinary strings, external/data/absolute URLs, and fragment-only references stay unchanged. It is not a full CSS parser: escaped function names and string-only image-set() references are unsupported; use url(...) for those references. There is no Sass/JavaScript compilation, bundling, or minification.

docs.title: Production builds
docs.text:
bin/flask assets:precompile
# From outside the application:
flaskteroids assets:precompile --root /path/to/app

These commands compile without application boot, database access, runtime keys, or initializers. Plain flask assets:precompile loads the app first.

Deploy the output directory with its .manifest.json. Builds are deterministic; helpers raise AssetError for missing/invalid manifests, missing entries, or missing compiled files. There is no source fallback. Docker includes compilation and retains output; generated Git/Docker exclusions omit build artifacts.

Flask serves the output directory directly, not a manifest allowlist. Old fingerprints remain usable after builds; compilation does not delete them. Keep only intended public files in asset directories. Hidden paths and symlinks are rejected; missing/unsafe HTTP requests return 404.

Generated production configuration sets Flask's SEND_FILE_MAX_AGE_DEFAULT to one year; successful compiled responses with positive cache lifetimes are also immutable. Set the native option to None for conditional revalidation or 0 for immediate revalidation. Without this configuration, Flask defaults to revalidation. The option also affects other send_file() calls without an explicit cache lifetime.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
config.assets.source_path = "app/assets"
config.assets.output_path = "public/assets"
config.assets.prefix = "/assets"
config.assets.serve = True

These select Flask's static_folder and static_url_path before registering its static route, which calls app.send_static_file directly. Paths are project-root-relative, must stay inside the project, and cannot overlap. One source root contains all asset types. URL prefixes must be absolute paths without query strings; trailing slashes are normalized.

For example, use source_path = "frontend", output_path = "static", and prefix = "/rails/assets" to change the directories and URL independently. The bootless compiler does not read Python configuration; pass matching paths:

bin/flask assets:precompile --source frontend --output static

Exclude custom output directories from Git/Docker input and regenerate them in the build. Helpers respect deployment script prefixes.

For reverse-proxy delivery, serve the output at the configured prefix and set config.assets.serve = False; URL generation remains available. Configure MIME and cache headers, block dotfiles (including the manifest) and symlinks, and never expose source/project directories.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: Attach uploaded files to models using disk or S3-compatible storage.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
To generate a resource with file uploads, run these commands inside your application:

flask generate scaffold User name:string avatar:attachment documents:attachments
flask attachments:install
flask db:migrate

Model, resource, and scaffold generators accept name:attachment for one file and name:attachments for multiple files. Here, avatar and documents are attachment names, not database columns. The scaffold generates the model declarations, upload inputs, controller parameters, and file links.

flask attachments:install creates an attachment migration and adds config/storage.yml if it is missing. flask db:migrate applies the model and attachment migrations.

docs.title: Add attachments to a model
docs.text:
To add attachments to an existing model without a generator, declare them with has_one_attached or has_many_attached. Run flask attachments:install and flask db:migrate if attachments have not been set up yet.

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_one_attached, has_many_attached


class User(ApplicationModel):
    has_one_attached('avatar')
    has_many_attached('documents')

Pass an uploaded file to attach, or include it in create or update:

user.avatar.attach(upload)
user.update(avatar=another_upload)
user.documents.attach(first_upload, second_upload)

attach appends to a collection. user.update(documents=[upload]) replaces it. For new records or records with unsaved changes, call save() after attaching.

You can also attach an open file:

with open("avatar.png", "rb") as stream:
    user.avatar.attach(io=stream, filename="avatar.png")

Use user.avatar.attached() to check for a file and user.avatar.filename to read its name. Files become available after commit: standalone saves and attaches to clean persisted records commit before returning; operations in an explicit Model.transaction() wait for that block to commit. In model callbacks, read new uploads in after_commit, not after_save. Standalone blob creation and explicit attachment removals also own a transaction unless joining an explicit block.

docs.title: Upload forms
docs.text:
{% call(form) form_with(model=user) %}
  {{ form.label("avatar") }}
  {{ form.file_field("avatar") }}

  {{ form.label("documents") }}
  {% for document in user.documents %}
    {{ form.hidden_field("documents", multiple=True, value=document.signed_id()) }}
  {% endfor %}
  {{ form.file_field("documents", multiple=True) }}
  {{ form.submit() }}
{% endcall %}

form_with handles multipart encoding. The hidden fields keep existing documents; without them, submitting the multiple file field replaces the collection, including clearing it when no files are selected. An empty single file input keeps the existing attachment.

Permit uploads in your controller:

attributes = params.expect(user=["avatar", ("documents", [])])
user.update(**attributes)

expect requires the outer user dictionary, not every permitted upload field. Keep a fixed allowlist: omitted fields are excluded from attributes, so a partial update leaves their attachments unchanged. To clear a collection, submit an empty list explicitly rather than omitting the field.

docs.title: Validation and limits
docs.text:
Replace the existing avatar declaration inside User with one that includes size and content-type checks. Keep its other declarations and methods:

from app.models.application_model import ApplicationModel
from flaskteroids.model import has_one_attached


class User(ApplicationModel):
    has_one_attached(
        "avatar",
        max_size=2 * 1024 * 1024,
        content_types=["image/png", "image/jpeg"],
    )

    # Keep other declarations and methods here.

Failed checks add messages to the model's errors and prevent saving. Content-type checks do not replace file scanning.

There is no per-file size limit by default. Set limits in your configuration:

config.attachments.max_upload_size = 20 * 1024 * 1024  # Per file
config["MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH"] = 25 * 1024 * 1024        # Entire request

Uploads over these limits return HTTP 413.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Edit config/storage.yml to define your services:

local:
  service: Disk
  root: storage

test:
  service: Disk
  root: tmp/storage

amazon:
  service: S3
  bucket: {env: S3_BUCKET}
  region: {env: AWS_REGION}

Relative disk paths start at the application root. Keep the storage directory persistent when deploying containers. Generated Docker applications use writable /app/storage for SQLite and local uploads; mount persistent storage there. Host bind mounts must be writable by the image user. bin/setup and default web startup create only conventional storage, not arbitrary configured directories.

For S3, install the optional dependency:

uv add "flaskteroids[s3]"

S3 uses your AWS credentials or IAM role. It also accepts endpoint and force_path_style for compatible providers.

Select a service in your environment configuration:

config.attachments.service = "amazon"

Generated applications use local in development and test in tests. Production uses ATTACHMENTS_SERVICE, defaulting to local. A declaration can override the default with service="amazon". Changing services does not move existing files.

docs.title: Download links
docs.text:
Use blob_path in templates:

{% if user.avatar.attached() %}
  <img src="{{ blob_path(user.avatar) }}" alt="Avatar">
{% endif %}

blob_path returns a relative link; blob_url returns an absolute URL. Both are also available from flaskteroids.attachments in Python. Use blob_path(user.avatar, disposition="attachment") to force a download, or pass expires_in=3600 for a link that expires after an hour.

Application links are permanent by default. user.avatar.url() returns a direct storage URL that normally expires after five minutes.

Anyone with a signed link can download the file by default. Only expose signed links and IDs to users allowed to access the file.

docs.title: Private files
docs.text:
Define can_download(blob) in app/helpers/permissions.py to check permissions and return True or False. Configure it in an initializer:

# config/initializers/attachments.py
from flask import current_app
from app.helpers.permissions import can_download

current_app.config.attachments.authorize = can_download
current_app.config.attachments.resolve_model_to_route = "proxy"

The callback can inspect blob.attachments to check ownership. Check the browser session in the callback; these routes do not run controller authentication callbacks. Denied downloads return 404.

Use blob_path or blob_url for private files. Direct storage URLs bypass the permission check, so avoid user.avatar.url() and public storage for those files.

docs.title: Remove files
docs.text:
user.avatar.detach()       # Keep the file, remove the attachment
user.avatar.purge_later()  # Delete the file in a background job
user.avatar.purge()        # Delete the file now

Replacing attachments or deleting their record schedules file deletion by default. Run your Celery worker to process these jobs. Shared files are not purged while another attachment uses them.

Prefer purge_later in transactions and callbacks. Rolling back after purge does not restore the deleted file.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
Place files in test/fixtures/files and attach them in your tests:

from test.test_helper import fixture_file_upload

user.avatar.attach(fixture_file_upload("avatar.png"))

Tests use temporary local storage, even when the application uses S3. Browser tests can use self.attach_file("Avatar", "test/fixtures/files/avatar.png"). See Testing for test setup.

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text: Run commands from your project directory with bin/flask—no environment activation needed. Use bin/flask --help to explore, or add --help to any command. You can also use flask in an activated environment, or uv run flask.

docs.title: Generation and setup
docs.text:
flaskteroids new my_app
cd my_app
bin/flask run
bin/flask test
bin/flask test:system

Your new app comes with its dependencies installed and development database ready. For a fresh checkout, run bin/setup before starting work.

Want to create the files first and install later? Use --skip-install, then run bin/setup when you're ready. Commit uv.lock so your team shares the same dependency versions.

docs.title: Asset precompilation
docs.text:
bin/flask assets:precompile
flaskteroids assets:precompile --root /path/to/app

Build assets for production. See Assets for the full workflow.

docs.title: Database preparation
docs.text:
As your models grow, migrations describe how their tables should change. Run db:prepare to create the database if needed and apply those migrations:

bin/flask db:prepare

To prepare another environment, choose it with FLASK_ENV:

FLASK_ENV=test bin/flask db:prepare
FLASK_ENV=production bin/flask db:prepare

Preparation doesn't reset the database or seed records. After successful migration, Flaskteroids regenerates db/schema.py from the selected database. Commit this read-only snapshot; do not duplicate column changes there by hand. Review migrations and the resulting snapshot before deploying: changes and rollbacks can delete data. Restart servers/workers afterward; published mappings are not modified in place.

Command When to use it db:prepare Get a database ready, or bring it up to date. db:create Create the database without applying migrations. db:migrate Apply pending migrations to an existing database. db:rollback Undo the most recent migration. db:init Add migration files to an app that doesn't have them yet. db:schema:dump Refresh db/schema.py from the selected database without changing data.

New apps already include migration files. If preparation fails, fix the reported problem and try again; the database is left in place for you to inspect. If migrations succeed but snapshot publication fails, fix the file/access problem and run bin/flask db:schema:dump; a failed file write does not undo applied migrations.

Commands use normal application initialization, including initializers. New model declarations can be imported before their snapshot tables exist. An initializer that actually constructs or queries an unavailable model still fails normally; there is no migration-only startup mode.

For PostgreSQL or MySQL, start the server and configure its connection first. For SQLite, use a database file rather than :memory: and make sure its parent directory exists.

docs.title: Shell
docs.text:
flask shell provides your models and session:

user = User.create(name="Alice")  # Commits before returning
with User.transaction():
    user.update(name="Alicia")
    User.create(name="Bob")
# Both changes commit at the end of the block.

Standalone save(), create(), update(), and destroy() commit immediately. Use Model.transaction() to group changes; saves join that explicit transaction, and an exception escaping the block rolls the group back. A False save result does not itself abort an explicit block. Shell exit rolls back unfinished work; it does not undo earlier standalone commits. Native writes require explicit commit/transaction handling. Use record.discard_changes() or record.reload() to discard staged input.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
Edit or inspect shared encrypted credentials:

flask credentials:edit
flask credentials:show

Use --environment for environment-specific credentials:

flask credentials:edit --environment production

See Configuration for encryption keys and credential precedence.

docs.title: Generators
docs.text: Use flask generate to create application components. Field arguments use name:type syntax. See Fields for supported types.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text: Generate a migration to create/drop a table or add/remove columns. New tables include an auto-incrementing id, created_at, and updated_at. Standalone migration generation does not edit the snapshot; applying the migration does.

docs.title: Create a table
docs.text:
flask generate migration <CreateXXX> [field1:type ...]

For example:

flask generate migration CreateProducts name:string!

Use the plural table name after Create, without a Table suffix.

docs.title: Add columns
docs.text:
flask generate migration <AddXXXToXXX> [field1:type ...]
flask generate migration AddPriceToProducts price:float

docs.title: Remove columns
docs.text:
flask generate migration <RemoveXXXFromXXX> [field1 ...]
flask generate migration RemovePriceFromProducts price

docs.title: Drop a table
docs.text:
flask generate migration <DropXXXX> [field1 ...]
flask generate migration DropProducts

Apply pending migrations with:

flask db:migrate

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
Generate a behavioral model, its database migration, and tests. References add belongs_to(...) declarations inside the model class. Columns appear in the generated snapshot only after migration:

flask generate model <ModelName> [field1:type ...]
flask generate model User name:string email:string

docs.title: Controller
docs.text:
Generate a controller with the specified actions, a view for each action, and individual route entries:

flask generate controller <ControllerName> [action1 action2 ...]
flask generate controller Users index show

This also creates app/helpers/users_helper.py with a UsersHelper class. Its public presentation methods are automatically available in templates; no controller registration is needed. See application helpers.

docs.title: Resource
docs.text:
Generate a model, its migration, an empty controller, and a resource route entry. You write the controller actions and views.

flask generate resource <ResourceName> [field1:type ...]

docs.title: Scaffold
docs.text:
Generate a model, its migration, a CRUD controller, views, and a resource route entry. The controller includes index, show, new, edit, create, update, and destroy actions.

flask generate scaffold <scaffold_name> [field1:type ...]

docs.title: Mailer
docs.text:
Generate a mailer with the specified actions:

flask generate mailer <MailerName> [action1 action2 ...]
flask generate mailer UserMailer welcome_email

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
flask generate authentication

Generate user and session models, login pages, and password management:

  • A User model with email_address and password_digest.
  • A Session model with user_id, ip_address, and user_agent.
  • Controllers and views for login and password changes.
  • Views and mailers for password resets.
  • Routes for session and password management.
  • An Authentication concern added to ApplicationController, requiring login by default and exposing the is_authenticated() template helper.

Run flask db:migrate, then create an account in the shell; no public sign-up form is generated. Use skip_before_action("_require_authentication", only=[...]) inside a controller class to allow public actions. Templates can call is_authenticated() on both public and protected pages without an extra callback. See the authentication walkthrough.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text:
Set up file attachments:

flask attachments:install
flask db:migrate

The install command preserves existing storage configuration and does not create duplicate migrations. Models, resources, and scaffolds accept avatar:attachment and documents:attachments. See Attachments.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Run model, integration, job, and mailer tests with flask test. Run browser tests with flask test:system. Both commands accept pytest arguments. See Testing for setup and examples.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Migration, model, resource, and scaffold generators accept these field types:

Type Generator argument Text text String (255 characters) string or str Integer integer or int Float float Boolean boolean or bool Date and time datetime Date date Time time JSON json 
flask generate model Post title:string! content:text published:boolean
flask db:prepare

! makes a database column non-nullable. author:references (or author:belongs_to) adds a required foreign key and a belongs_to(...) declaration inside the generated model class. Database constraints do not replace user-facing validation; add validates(...) inside the model class when invalid input should return errors rather than a native constraint exception.

Generators use SQLAlchemy type factories. They do not maintain a second input casting API. Migrations define the database; the generated db/schema.py snapshot supplies mapped column types. Do not edit it to change a field.

docs.title: Model casting and raw input
docs.text:
Casting happens at model assignment, not only in forms or at database bind time. Scalar input remains staged until saved. Read it through normal attributes, and inspect original input with read_attribute_before_type_cast(name).

  • String/text values stringify ordinary input; None remains None.
  • Integers accept numeric strings and numeric prefixes ("12extra" reads as 12). Blank input reads as None; nonnumeric strings read as zero but serialize as null. Add numericality validation to reject malformed original input.
  • Float/decimal values cast numeric strings; blank input reads as None.
  • Booleans cast "" to None. False values include False, 0, "0", "f", "F", "false", "FALSE", "off", and "OFF"; other non-null values are true.
  • Dates/times accept ISO-formatted strings and corresponding Python values. Invalid date/time strings read as None; the original input is retained for validation and form redisplay.
  • JSON values retain their Python structure and native SQLAlchemy serialization. Supported backend-specific types use SQLAlchemy's native database handling.
post = Post.new(word_count="12extra")
assert post.word_count == 12
assert post.read_attribute_before_type_cast("word_count") == "12extra"
# validates("word_count", numericality={"only_integer": True}) rejects this input.

docs.title: Nulls and defaults
docs.text:
Explicit None remains null for ordinary scalar columns, even when a server default exists. An omitted value can instead use the default. Simple literal server defaults are decoded for new model instances without database I/O; server functions and computed values populate on flush. Put persistent defaults in migrations; Python-side default functions cannot be recovered from a snapshot.

JSON's default serialization stores explicit None as JSON null, which reads back as None. JSON null is distinct from SQL NULL; an SQL IS NULL predicate does not necessarily match it. Primary-key generation remains native.

docs.title: Attachments
docs.text: Model, resource, and scaffold generators accept avatar:attachment for a single file and documents:attachments for multiple files. These declare attachments, not scalar columns. Run flask attachments:install, then migrate and regenerate the snapshot through flask db:migrate. See Attachments.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text: Use form_with to build model-backed forms and self.params.expect to filter submitted attributes.

docs.title: Building forms
docs.text:
form_with(model=post) chooses the form's action and HTTP method from the model and includes a CSRF token. Inside the template block, it exposes a Form object for generating labels and inputs:

<!-- app/views/posts/_form.html -->
{% call(form) form_with(model=post) %}
  <div>
    {{ form.label('title') }}
    {{ form.text_field('title') }}
  </div>

  <div>
    {{ form.label('content') }}
    {{ form.text_area('content') }}
  </div>

  <div>
    {{ form.submit('Save') }}
  </div>
{% endcall %}

docs.title: Destinations and HTTP methods
docs.text:
New records infer their collection URL and POST. Persisted records infer their member URL and PATCH, rendered as POST with a hidden _method. An explicit method always wins; method="PUT" remains supported for an update.

An explicit URL changes only the destination. The model still supplies values, errors, and default method inference:

{% call(form) form_with(model=post, url="/review", method="POST") %}
  {{ form.text_field("title") }}
  {{ form.submit("Review") }}
{% endcall %}

With a persisted post, omitting method="POST" here would infer PATCH, not POST. url=None (or omission) permits inference; url=False omits action; url="" keeps an explicit empty action targeting the current page.

Ordinary nested model destinations accept a list or tuple:

{% call(form) form_with(model=[product, subscriber]) %}
  {{ form.email_field("email") }}
  {{ form.submit("Subscribe") }}
{% endcall %}

A new child submits to product_subscribers_path(product) with POST; a persisted child submits to product_subscriber_path(product, subscriber) with PATCH. Fields use the child prefix (subscriber[email]) and child values, including rejected input. scope="signup" overrides that prefix without changing the value/error-owning model. Missing ancestor identities fail diagnostically. Nested URLs do not enable nested-attribute mass assignment or persistence.

Field helpers include text_field, text_area, password_field, and checkbox. Use file_field('avatar') or file_field('documents', multiple=True) for uploads. form_with detects these fields and adds multipart encoding. See Attachments for attachment forms and permitted parameters.

docs.title: Buttons that submit forms
docs.text:
{{ button_to("Create", "/products") }}
{{ button_to("Save", product) }}
{{ button_to("Delete", product, method="DELETE") }}
{{ button_to("Log out", session_path(), method="DELETE") }}

The default is POST for an explicit URL or new record and PATCH for a persisted record. Nested model sequences infer from the final record, just like forms. Deletion is always explicit. GET and POST render native HTML methods; PUT/PATCH/DELETE render POST plus the corresponding hidden override. GET forms include neither CSRF tokens nor method overrides, preventing tokens in query strings. Unsafe forms include a CSRF token.

Button attributes and form attributes are separate:

{{ button_to("Save", product, id="save-button", form={"id": "save-form", "class": "inline"}) }}

Labels and attributes are escaped; trusted Markup is permitted for labels, not unescaped attributes. Unsupported/executable destination schemes are rejected. Action omission, arbitrary extra hidden button parameters, and remote/Turbo options are not part of this bounded button API.

docs.title: Form values and escaping
docs.text:
Model-backed forms use before-type-cast scalar input and assigned writable virtual fields, falling back to published mapped values. Failed validation therefore keeps the original submission available even when a cast would lose information. Authentication secrets, digests, confirmations, and reset tokens are excluded by default. Forms do not use JSON response serialization or evaluate read-only virtual fields such as reset tokens. Re-enter passwords after an unsuccessful submission.

Field names, prefixes, attribute values, input values, and textarea values are escaped. Keep field names and attribute names application-defined. Invalid HTML attribute names raise ValueError. Do not construct field attributes from unfiltered request data.

collection_select() escapes ordinary option labels and prompts. Explicit markupsafe.Markup is accepted for trusted labels and prompts, but option values and other field values are always escaped, even when supplied as Markup.

Form actions accept relative URLs, including protocol-relative URLs, and HTTP(S) URLs. Other schemes and URLs containing control characters raise ValueError. This policy prevents executable schemes; it does not restrict which hosts a form may submit to. Check destinations separately if they come from user input.

docs.title: Strong parameters
docs.text:
Use self.params.expect to select the attributes a controller may pass to a model. Do not pass unfiltered request data to create or update. Otherwise, users could change attributes you did not intend to expose, such as an admin flag.

expect checks the expected structure, including nested objects and lists. For a post form:

# app/controllers/posts_controller.py
from flaskteroids.controller import ActionController
from flaskteroids.routes import post_path
from app.models.post import Post

class PostsController(ActionController):
    # ...

    def create(self):
        self.post = Post.new(**self._post_params())
        if self.post.save():
            return self.redirect_to(post_path(self.post))
        return self.render('new', status=422)

    def update(self):
        self.post = Post.find(self.params['id'])
        if self.post.update(**self._post_params()):
            return self.redirect_to(post_path(self.post))
        return self.render('edit', status=422)

    def _post_params(self):
        # Assumes form data is sent as:
        # post[title]=...
        # post[content]=...
        return self.params.expect(post=['title', 'content'])

self.params.expect(post=['title', 'content']) requires a top-level post dictionary, but its nested fields are permitted, not required. It returns only submitted, permitted attributes and discards other attributes. The same allowlist works for both creation and partial updates:

# Submitted: post[content]=Updated
attributes = self.params.expect(post=['title', 'content'])
# attributes == {'content': 'Updated'}
post.update(**attributes)  # The existing title is unchanged.

This also applies recursively to nested dictionaries and arrays of dictionaries. Omitted fields are not filled with defaults; an explicitly submitted None scalar is retained. Use model validations to require attributes, rather than treating the allowlist as validation.

Missing, null, or empty roots raise MissingParameter, including dictionaries with no permitted attributes after filtering. Required scalar roots, such as self.params.expect('password'), reject blank strings but accept False and numeric zero. Incorrect supplied types raise InvalidParameter; making fields optional does not relax the expected structure.

During HTTP requests, Flaskteroids automatically translates MissingParameter and InvalidParameter into 400 Bad Request responses; controllers do not need to catch them. The default response is an HTML error page, including when JSON is requested. Applications can customize either response with Flask's register_error_handler() in an initializer (for example, to return JSON). Direct calls outside request dispatch still raise these exceptions. Programmer errors and unrelated exceptions are not translated into 400 responses.

docs.title: CSRF protection
docs.text:
Flaskteroids checks CSRF tokens on state-changing requests, meaning all methods except GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE. form_with and button_to include the token for unsafe forms, never GET forms. An overridden DELETE receives the same protection as an actual DELETE request. See Routing.

Tokens belong to the browser session and expire after one hour. Clearing the session invalidates its tokens; reload forms to obtain a new token. AJAX requests can send the token in the X-CSRF-TOKEN header instead of the csrf_token form field. Do not store pages containing CSRF tokens in a shared cache.

Include the token yourself in manual forms:

<form action="/posts" method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="csrf_token" value="{{ csrf_token() }}">
  <!-- ... form fields -->
</form>

docs.title: Background jobs
docs.text:
Jobs inherit from Job and define perform. Use them for work that should run outside the HTTP request, such as processing an upload.

# app/jobs/my_job.py
from flaskteroids.jobs.job import Job

class MyJob(Job):
    def perform(self, user_id):
        # Do some long-running task
        print(f"Performing job for user {user_id}")

To enqueue a job, call perform_later:

MyJob().perform_later(user_id=1)

Jobs in app/jobs are registered automatically. Call perform_later inside an application context. Requests already have one; see using models and jobs in scripts for standalone code.

docs.title: Mailers
docs.text:
Mailers inherit from ActionMailer. Each action sets template variables and calls mail with the recipient and subject.

# app/mailers/user_mailer.py
from flaskteroids.mailer import ActionMailer

class UserMailer(ActionMailer):
    def welcome_email(self):
        self.user = self.params["user"]
        return self.mail(to=self.user.email, subject="Welcome to My App!")

Call deliver_now to send the email immediately, or deliver_later to enqueue a background job:

# Deliver now
UserMailer.with_params(user=user).welcome_email().deliver_now()

# Deliver later using a background job
UserMailer.with_params(user=user).welcome_email().deliver_later()

docs.title: Parameterized mailers
docs.text:
with_params(...) supplies action and callback inputs through self.params, an instance-owned dictionary that needs no HTTP request. Each action call gets a fresh mailer and a shallow parameter copy. Action arguments remain supported.

Input params are not automatically template assigns. Expose values needed by templates and delivery-time helpers explicitly, as with self.user above.

docs.title: Mailer helper methods
docs.text:
Use helper_method to expose a private mailer method to its templates:

from flaskteroids.mailer import ActionMailer, helper_method


class NoticesMailer(ActionMailer):
    helper_method("_greeting")

    def welcome(self, name, email):
        self.name = name
        return self.mail(to=email, subject="Welcome")

    def _greeting(self, punctuation="!"):
        return f"Hello, {self.name}{punctuation}"

<!-- app/views/notices_mailer/welcome.html -->
<p>{{ greeting() }}</p>

The declaration is inherited and uses child overrides. Positional and keyword arguments are forwarded to the mailer method. Private methods are not mailer actions or template helpers unless explicitly exposed. Returned text is escaped normally in HTML templates.

helper(...) has a different purpose: it includes presentation helper classes in the view context, whose methods can call self.greeting(). Mailers select those classes explicitly rather than inheriting request-controller helpers. See application helpers.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Actions and callbacks run immediately, capturing the recipient and subject. deliver_now() renders the supplied objects. deliver_later() stores saved model assigns as references and reloads them at delivery, including models nested in lists, tuples, and dictionaries. Other queued assigns must be serializable by the queue adapter.

Unsaved model assigns raise SerializationError on enqueue; records missing at delivery raise DeserializationError (both in flaskteroids.exceptions). Queued rendering ignores unsaved edits without altering the caller's objects. Enqueue after commit so records are visible to the worker.

Text and HTML parts share one delivery-time mailer. Unlike Rails, queued delivery does not rerun the action, so model-backed template values can change while the captured headers remain fixed.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
Views are Jinja2 templates in app/views. By default, a controller action renders the template matching its controller and action name. For example, PostsController.index renders app/views/posts/index.html.

Controller instance variables become template variables. If the action sets self.posts, the template can use posts:

<!-- app/views/posts/index.html -->
{% extends "layouts/application.html" %}

{% block body %}
<h1>Posts</h1>

<ul>
  {% for post in posts %}
  <li>{{ post.title }}</li>
  {% endfor %}
</ul>
{% endblock %}

docs.title: Application helpers
docs.text:
Put reusable presentation methods in helper classes under app/helpers. The application generator creates ApplicationHelper; the controller generator also creates a matching helper class.

For example:

# app/helpers/products_helper.py
class ProductsHelper:
    def product_link(self, product):
        return self.link_to(product.name, self.product_path(product))

Use it directly in a view, layout, or partial:

{{ product_link(product) }}

By default, all conventional helper classes are available in every controller's views. No import, callback, or helper_method declaration is needed.

docs.title: Discovery and the view context
docs.text:
config.paths.helpers defaults to the Python package "app.helpers". Each *_helper.py file must define its matching class: products_helper.py defines ProductsHelper, and admin/money_helper.py defines MoneyHelper. Nested directories can be namespace packages without __init__.py.

Only these conventional files are automatically imported. Private paths (starting with _) are skipped. A missing helper package is allowed; syntax errors, missing dependencies, and incorrectly named classes in existing helper files stop application startup.

Helper classes act as mixins on a shared view context, not separately constructed objects. Do not define __init__; initialize any render-local state lazily. Public methods become callable template helpers. Private _methods remain available to other helper methods through self, but are not exported to templates.

Within a helper, self can access: - Other included helper methods. - Framework and route helpers, such as self.link_to(...) and self.product_path(product). - Explicitly exposed methods on the current controller or delivery-time mailer. - Controller or mailer instance variables, such as self.product. Controller views can also use request facilities such as self.params and self.request.

Pass template-local values as arguments. Helpers do not become controller methods or actions. Helper instance state is shared across the current view, layout, and calls to render(...), but does not survive a separate render or request. Use self.render(...) to render a partial from another helper.

docs.title: Restricting automatic inclusion
docs.text:
To include shared application helpers and only conventionally matching controller helpers, configure:

config.action_controller.include_all_helpers = False

For example, ProductsController receives ApplicationHelper and ProductsHelper. Child controllers inherit their parents' helper selections and add their own matching helper. Namespaced controllers match namespaced helper paths.

Include other helper classes explicitly inside the controller class:

from app.controllers.application_controller import ApplicationController
from app.helpers.formatting_helper import FormattingHelper
from flaskteroids.controller import helper


class ProductsController(ApplicationController):
    helper(FormattingHelper, "admin/money")

Names such as "formatting", "FormattingHelper", and "admin/money" resolve against the configured helper package. helper("all") explicitly includes all discovered helpers.

This mirrors Rails' distinction: helper(...) includes presentation helpers in the view context; helper_method(...) delegates a particular method to the current controller or delivery-time mailer.

docs.title: Method precedence
docs.text:
Conventional helpers are included before explicit declarations at each controller level. Automatic inclusion of all helpers happens at the root controller level in sorted helper-path order, with ApplicationHelper included first. Later includes take precedence, but including an already-included class does not move it.

A controller or mailer's helper_method declarations override helper mixins included at that same level. A child's helper layer can override inherited methods. Ordinary Python super() works between helper mixins. Application helpers can override framework helpers; prefer unique names unless an override is intentional.

docs.title: Mailers and rendering outside requests
docs.text:
Mailer templates do not inherit the current request controller's helper methods or automatically include every application helper. Include the classes they need explicitly:

from app.mailers.application_mailer import ApplicationMailer
from flaskteroids.mailer import helper


class NoticesMailer(ApplicationMailer):
    helper("application", "formatting")
    # Mailer actions go here.

A conventionally matching NoticesMailerHelper, if defined in notices_mailer_helper.py, is also included. Mailer instance variables are available to helpers through self. These selections apply to immediate and queued delivery. Mailers can also expose their own private methods with helper_method, imported from flaskteroids.mailer. These declarations are inherited, honor overridden methods, and accept arguments just like controller helper methods. They delegate to the mailer, never to a request controller.

The existing mail pipeline captures assigns rather than rerunning mailer actions at delivery. One mailer instance is restored from those assigns per message, without rerunning its constructor, actions, or callbacks. Its helper methods share that instance across text and HTML parts. Queued assigns must satisfy the queue adapter's serialization requirements. See mailer helpers.

Standalone Flask template rendering inside an application context uses all application helpers by default, or just ApplicationHelper when include_all_helpers is false. Controller delegates are unavailable without a current request controller. Request-dependent helpers still require a request; URL generation outside a request follows Flask's normal configuration rules. Jinja macros imported without context do not receive render-local helpers; import them with context when needed.

docs.title: Development changes
docs.text: Helper modules are imported at application boot. Use bin/flask run --debug for Flask's process reloader, or restart the server after changing Python helpers. The framework does not perform a separate in-process module reload. config.enable_reloading enables template reloading but does not, by itself, reload Python helper code.

docs.title: Helper escaping and URLs
docs.text:
link_to() and button_to() escape ordinary text and HTML attribute values. Use markupsafe.Markup only for HTML you trust, such as an application-defined icon or label. Never mark user input safe. Attributes are escaped even when supplied as Markup.

link_to() accepts relative URLs, including protocol-relative URLs, and the http, https, mailto, and tel schemes. Form helpers accept relative and HTTP(S) action URLs. Unsupported schemes, such as javascript and data, and URLs containing control characters raise ValueError. HTML escaping alone does not make an executable URL safe.

These checks do not restrict destination hosts. Applications must validate user-supplied destinations when links or forms should stay on a particular site. Keep HTML attribute names application-defined. Invalid names raise ValueError; valid event-handler attributes still contain executable code and must never come from untrusted input.
